title: Home Economics literacy, family and consumer life skills (exploratory)
md:
# HE-A2 — Home Economics literacy, family and consumer life skills

Annex F gives this exploratory course **11 items** (Remember 1, Understand 2, Apply 5, Analyze 2, Evaluate 1). Its outcomes list: why HE matters; hygiene and grooming; nutritious meals; household resource management; fabrics and textiles; sewing a simple garment and repairs; marriage and family; family roles, functions and life cycle; informed buying; saving and managing income; conflict resolution and parenting basics. [SRC-0002, Annex F, A.2]

This is the **introductory** version of the HE major. The deeper versions are HE-B1 (home management, consumer laws), HE-B2 (food and nutrition), HE-B4 (family and child) and HE-B6 (clothing). This lesson covers what those do not: hygiene, fibers and fabrics, simple sewing and care, saving, and family conflict.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Why HE matters.** Home Economics teaches the everyday skills of a household: keeping clean, feeding a family well, managing money and things, dressing, and getting along. At the exploratory level, learners try each area before choosing a specialization.

**Hygiene and food safety.** Clean hands stop germs moving from person to person and from raw food to cooked food. The four steps of safe food handling are **clean, separate, cook, chill**.

**Fibers and fabrics.** Fabric is made from fibers. Fibers are **natural** (from plants, animals or minerals), **synthetic** (made from petrochemicals, like nylon and polyester), or **semi-synthetic** (natural cellulose that is chemically processed, like rayon). Plant fibers are classed by the part of the plant they come from.

**Philippine fabrics.** The Philippines is known for **piña** (pineapple leaf) and **abacá** (Manila hemp) fabrics, used in the barong tagalog. A 2004 law requires Philippine tropical fabrics for government uniforms.

**Simple sewing and care.** Check the fabric, follow its grain when laying patterns, sew, then finish (hems, closures) and press at the right heat. Know the common machine faults.

**Money.** Budget first, then save. A savings account is flexible but earns little interest. Keep an emergency fund.

**Family.** Marriage under the Family Code is a permanent union and the foundation of the family. Parent–teen conflict is normal, usually mild, and part of how roles are renegotiated.

## 2. Testable facts

**Hygiene and food handling**
- The four key steps in handling, preparing and serving food: **clean, separate, cook, chill**. [SRC-0108, Ch. 17 "Efforts on the consumer level"]
- Wash hands with **warm, soapy water for at least 20 seconds** before preparing food and after handling raw foods; this prevents cross-contamination and person-to-person spread. [SRC-0108, Ch. 17 "Efforts on the consumer level"]
- Never thaw meat, poultry or seafood at **room temperature**; thaw in the refrigerator, microwave, or a sealed bag in cold water. [SRC-0108, Ch. 17 "Efforts on the consumer level"]
- A cutting board can be sanitized with about **1 teaspoon (5 mL) of chlorine bleach per 1 litre of water**; use separate boards for produce and raw meat. [SRC-0108, Ch. 17 "Efforts on the consumer level"]

**Fibers**
- Fibers fall into three groups: **natural, synthetic, semi-synthetic**. Natural fibers come from plants, animals and minerals (e.g. cotton, wool, silk, linen). [SRC-0141, paragraph on fiber categories]
- Plant fibers by source: **seed** fiber (cotton); **leaf** fiber (pineapple, abacá/banana); **bast** fiber from the stem's outer layer (flax, jute, ramie, kenaf, hemp). [SRC-0140, "Plant fibers"]
- **Animal fibers are proteins** (e.g. keratin in wool, fibroin in silk). **Silk** is secreted by insects making cocoons. [SRC-0140, "Animal fibers"]
- **Rayon (viscose)** is regenerated cellulose; the first successful viscose process dates from **1894** (Cross, Bevan and Beadle). [SRC-0141, "The first synthetic fibers"]
- **Nylon** was the first fully synthetic fiber, developed by **Wallace Carothers** at DuPont (nylon 66 first made in 1935). [SRC-0141, "The first synthetic fibers"]
- Of all fibers, **cotton** dominates textile production and use among natural fibers. [SRC-0140, "Industrial use"]

**Philippine fabrics**
- **Piña** is a traditional Philippine fiber from **pineapple leaves**, woven into sheer *nipis* fabric for the barong tagalog and baro't saya. [SRC-0142, lead and "History"]
- **Aklan piña handloom weaving** was inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in **2023**. [SRC-0142, infobox]
- **Abacá** (*Musa textilis*, "Manila hemp") is a banana species **endemic to the Philippines**; the **Bicol region** has the most cultivars. [SRC-0143, lead and "Genetic diversity"]
- Per the Fiber Industry Development Authority (as reported), the Philippines supplied about **87%** of the world's abacá in 2014. [SRC-0143, "Cultivation"]
- **RA 9242 (2004), Philippine Tropical Fabrics Law:** tropical fabrics are those containing **natural fibers produced, spun, woven or knitted and finished in the Philippines**; they are prescribed for **official uniforms of government officials and employees**. [SRC-0050, Secs. 2–3]
- RA 9242 funds the **Fiber Industry Development Authority (FIDA)** of the Department of Agriculture to promote plant-fiber production; the **Civil Service Commission** issues the implementing rules. [SRC-0050, Secs. 5–6]

**Fabric care and simple sewing (TESDA Dressmaking NC II)**
- Before cutting, fabric is checked for **quality, faults, width and selvedges**, and soaked or drip-dried and pressed according to standard fabric care. [SRC-0080, "Prepare and cut materials", element 1 and range of variables]
- Patterns are laid out and pinned **according to the fabric grain line**, and seam allowances are marked. [SRC-0080, "Prepare and cut materials", element 2]
- Standard fabric care methods listed: **dry cleaning, soaking and drying, machine washing, tumble-drying**. [SRC-0080, "Prepare and cut materials", range of variables 3]
- Common sewing-machine faults: **puckering, uneven stitch, loose threads, skipping stitch**. [SRC-0080, "Sew casual apparel", range of variables 2]
- Pressing tools: **flat iron, ironing board, sleeve board, press mitt, tailor's ham**. Heat levels given: **Level 1 silk, Level 2 cotton, Level 3 maong (denim)**. [SRC-0080, "Apply finishing touches", range of variables 2 and 4]
- Finishing touches include **closures, hemming, accessories and accents, stitches**. [SRC-0080, "Apply finishing touches", range of variables 1]

**Saving and managing income**
- Three main savings vehicles: **savings account, certificate of deposit (time deposit), money market account**. [SRC-0090, 6.6]
- A savings account is **flexible** (deposits and withdrawals anytime) but earns **low interest**, so it is poor for growing money. [SRC-0090, 6.6]
- Experts recommend keeping savings to cover **3 to 6 months of living expenses** as an emergency fund. [SRC-0090, 6.6]
- A budget starts by listing income, then **categorizing expenses** (housing, food, transport…) and comparing the two. [SRC-0090, 6.5]

**Marriage, family and conflict**
- The Family Code defines marriage as a **special contract of permanent union** between a man and a woman, the **foundation of the family** and an inviolable social institution. [SRC-0071, Art. 1]
- An **extended family** household includes at least one parent and child plus other relatives such as grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. [SRC-0088, 14.1]
- Contrary to popular belief, many families get along well in adolescence; warmth and closeness are especially common in **authoritative** households. [SRC-0087, 10.5]
- Parent–adolescent conflict is linked to teens' growing **autonomy**, new reasoning skills and changing roles; it can both drive and result from the redefinition of the relationship. [SRC-0087, 10.5]

**Basic weaves (Stage 7 addition; Wikipedia, tertiary)**
- The **three fundamental weaves** are **plain, twill and satin**. [SRC-0256, lead; SRC-0257, lead]
- **Plain weave** is the most basic (simple over-under); fabrics are generally **strong and durable** with a smooth surface. [SRC-0256, lead]
- **Twill** has a pattern of **parallel diagonal ribs**; it is used for sturdy work clothing, and **denim is a twill**. [SRC-0257, lead]
- **Satin weave** has **long floats** (yarns floating over four or more crossing yarns), giving a **glossy, smooth** face and a dull back; it is **not very durable** because floats snag. [SRC-0255, lead]

**Fabric construction and finishes (Stage 7 addition; Wikipedia, tertiary)**
- **Weaving** interlaces two sets of yarns **at right angles**: lengthwise **warp** and crosswise **weft**. [SRC-0267, lead]
- **Knitting** interloops a **continuous length of yarn** into rows of **connected loops**. [SRC-0264, lead]
- **Felt** is made by **matting, condensing and pressing fibers** together (no weaving or knitting); in wet felting, hot water with **agitation and compression** makes wool fibers mat. [SRC-0265, lead and "Wet felting"]
- **Mercerisation** treats cotton (and flax) to improve **dye uptake and tear strength**, reduce shrinkage and give a **silk-like luster**; devised by **John Mercer in 1844**. [SRC-0266, lead and "Development"]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Rayon is not "fully synthetic".** It is semi-synthetic (regenerated cellulose). Nylon was the first fully synthetic fiber.
- **Piña vs abacá.** Piña comes from the *pineapple* leaf; abacá from a *banana* relative. Both are leaf fibers. Cotton is a *seed* fiber; flax/linen and jute are *bast* (stem) fibers.
- **Silk and wool are protein fibers**, not cellulose. (Relevant to care: protein fibers need low heat; silk is pressing Level 1.)
- **Thawing on the counter** is wrong, even if it is "faster".
- **Savings account = safe and flexible, not high-growth.**
- **Teen–parent conflict** is not a sign that a family is failing; constant severe conflict is the exception.
- **Denim is twill, not plain weave.** Satin's shine comes from floats, not from the fiber.
- **Felt is non-woven.** Hot water plus agitation is exactly what mats (felts) wool, which is why wool is washed gently in cool water.

## 4. Memory aid

**Fibers "SLB-P":** **S**eed = cotton, **L**eaf = piña/abacá, **B**ast = flax/jute; **P**rotein = silk/wool.
**Food safety "Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill."**
**Weaves "Plain = Plus sign, Twill = Tilt, Satin = Slide"** (over-under, diagonal, long floats).
**"Weave = Cross, Knit = Loop, Felt = Press."**

## 5. Sources

title: Introduction to ICT — hardware, software, productivity tools and responsible digital citizenship
md:
# HE-A3 — Introduction to ICT

Annex F gives this exploratory course **10 items** (Remember 1, Understand 2, Apply 5, Analyze 1, Evaluate 1). Outcomes: computing, science and math knowledge; **hardware and software components**; **responsible digital citizenship** (data privacy, online safety, ethics); **productivity software**; uses and **categories of application software**. [SRC-0002, Annex F, A.3]

## 1. Plain explanation

**A computer** is a programmable machine that follows stored instructions. Every computer works through the **information processing cycle: input → processing → output → storage**.

**Hardware** is the physical part: the motherboard, the CPU (the "brain"), memory and storage. **RAM** is temporary working memory that clears when power is off. **ROM** holds the start-up instructions. Hard disks, flash drives and cloud storage are **secondary (permanent) storage**.

**Software** has two big families. **System software** runs the computer (the operating system, drivers, antivirus). **Application software** does the user's tasks: word processing, spreadsheets, presentations, databases, browsers, and specialized programs.

**Networks** connect two or more devices: PAN (personal), LAN (local), WAN (wide). Routers direct traffic between networks.

**Digital citizenship** means using technology safely, securely, ethically and legally. In the Philippines that includes the **Data Privacy Act (RA 10173)**, the **Cybercrime Prevention Act (RA 10175)** and the **Intellectual Property Code (RA 8293)**.

## 2. Testable facts

**Hardware and processing (OpenStax Workplace Software and Skills 1.2)**
- Computers store programs and data as strings of **1s and 0s**. One binary digit is a **bit**; **8 bits make a byte**; a megabyte is a little over a million bytes. [SRC-0103, 5.1]
- A computer is a **programmable machine** that executes predefined lists of instructions and responds to new instructions. [SRC-0102, 1.2]
- The **motherboard** runs communications for the system and sits in the **system unit**; the **CPU** contains the **microprocessor**, the "brains", with a control unit and an **arithmetic-logic unit**. [SRC-0102, 1.2 "How Computers Work"]
- Information processing cycle: **input, processing, output, storage**. [SRC-0102, 1.2 "Information Processing"]
- **Primary storage = RAM**: temporary, short-term, available only while the computer is on; more RAM means programs run faster. **Secondary storage** (hard disks, flash drives, CDs) is permanent. [SRC-0102, 1.2]
- **ROM** holds hardwired instructions the computer needs **before the operating system loads**. [SRC-0102, 1.2]
- The **operating system** controls memory and processes, lets hardware and software communicate, and gives the user an interface (e.g. Windows, macOS, Android). [SRC-0102, 1.2 "Operating Systems"]
- Networks: **PAN** (devices in a small area), **LAN** (e.g. a campus linking computers and printers), **WAN** (large regions; the internet is the largest). A **router** directs traffic between networks and lets several computers share one internet connection. [SRC-0102, 1.2 "Networks"]
- A **client** requests resources on a network; a **server** connects devices and shares resources. [SRC-0102, 1.2 "Network Servers"]

**Software (2.1)**
- Two major categories: **system software** (operating system, printer and keyboard drivers, **antivirus**) and **application software** (task-oriented programs). **Web browsers** are application programs. [SRC-0102, 2.1]
- Program interface parts: **GUI**; **menu bar / ribbon** (general commands, top); **toolbar** (icons for common commands); **dialog box** (gives information or asks for input); **status bar** (bottom; e.g. page count). [SRC-0102, 2.1]
- Productivity applications: **word processing** (text documents: memos, letters, reports), **spreadsheet** (organize and analyze numeric data, charts), **presentation** (slideshows of text and graphics), **database** (organize and store large amounts of data). [SRC-0102, 2.1 "Common Applications"]
- **Specialized applications** serve particular occupations (e.g. accounting software); **mobile applications** are designed for phones and tablets. [SRC-0102, 2.1]

**Online safety and ethics (1.4)**
- **Computer security** protects systems and information from unauthorized use; **computer ethics** are guidelines for morally acceptable use; **cybercrime** is any criminal offense involving a computer and a network. [SRC-0102, 1.4]
- Protective strategies: security suites, a **firewall** (barrier between a secured and an unsecured network), password-protected network access, avoiding logins on **open networks**, and **encryption**. [SRC-0102, 1.4]
- **Phishing** lures users to fake emails or sites to give personal information; it usually relies on **spoofing** (messages that look as if they come from a trusted source). [SRC-0102, 1.4 "Data and Identity Theft"]
- Strong passwords: at least **eight characters**, mix letters and numbers, upper and lower case and symbols; no real names or whole words; **do not reuse**. **Biometrics** (fingerprints, retinal scans) are harder to steal. [SRC-0102, 1.4 "Password Management and Biometrics"]
- **Cookies** are small data files websites leave on your device to track browsing and search history. [SRC-0102, 1.4 "Cookies"]

**Data Privacy Act of 2012 (RA 10173)**
- **Personal information:** information from which a person's identity is apparent or can be reasonably and directly ascertained, or that identifies them when combined with other information. [SRC-0045, Sec. 3(g)]
- **Sensitive personal information** includes race, ethnic origin, marital status, age, religion, political affiliation; **health, education**, genetic or sexual life; government-issued numbers such as **SSS numbers, health records, licenses, tax returns**. [SRC-0045, Sec. 3(l)]
- **Consent** must be freely given, specific and informed, evidenced by written, electronic or recorded means. [SRC-0045, Sec. 3(b)]
- Processing follows the principles of **transparency, legitimate purpose and proportionality**. [SRC-0045, Sec. 11]
- Rights of the data subject include: to be **informed**; **reasonable access**; to **dispute** and have errors **corrected**; to have data **blocked, removed or destroyed** when incomplete, outdated, false or unlawfully obtained; and to be **indemnified** for damages. [SRC-0045, Sec. 16]
- The law creates the **National Privacy Commission** as an independent body to administer it. [SRC-0045, Sec. 7]

**Cybercrime Prevention Act of 2012 (RA 10175)**
- Offenses against confidentiality, integrity and availability: **illegal access**, **illegal interception**, **data interference** and **system interference** (both include introducing **viruses**), **misuse of devices**, **cyber-squatting** (bad-faith domain names). [SRC-0046, Sec. 4(a)]
- Computer-related offenses: **forgery, fraud, identity theft**. Content-related offenses: **cybersex, child pornography, unsolicited commercial communications, libel** (Revised Penal Code Art. 355 libel committed through a computer system). [SRC-0046, Sec. 4(b)–(c)]
- Crimes under the Revised Penal Code and special laws committed **through ICT** carry a penalty **one degree higher**. [SRC-0046, Sec. 6]

**Intellectual property (RA 8293)**
- **Computer programs** are protected literary and artistic works, protected **from the moment of creation**. [SRC-0044, Sec. 172.1(n)]
- The lawful owner of a program may make **one back-up copy** or adaptation without the copyright owner's permission, when needed for use or archival purposes. [SRC-0044, Sec. 189.1]
- Copyright generally lasts for the **author's life plus 50 years**. [SRC-0044, Sec. 213.1]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **RAM vs ROM.** RAM is temporary working memory (lost at power-off). ROM holds start-up instructions. Neither is "the hard disk".
- **Antivirus is system software**, not an application; a **browser is an application**.
- **Storage is the last step** of the IPOS cycle, after output.
- **Age, education and health are sensitive personal information** under RA 10173, not ordinary information.
- **Online libel** is punished under RA 10175 (via RPC Art. 355), one degree higher than ordinary libel.
- **Phishing vs spoofing.** Spoofing is the disguise (a fake sender); phishing is the lure to steal data.
- **Registration is not needed** for copyright; it exists from creation.

## 4. Memory aid

**"I Process Output Saved"** = Input, Processing, Output, Storage.
**Data subject rights "I-A-C-E-D":** Informed, Access, Correct, Erase/block, Damages.

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0102 OpenStax *Workplace Software and Skills* (2023) 1.2, 1.4, 2.1 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
- SRC-0103 OpenStax *Introduction to Computer Science* 5.1
- SRC-0045 RA 10173 (Secs. 3, 7, 11, 16)
- SRC-0046 RA 10175 (Secs. 4, 6)
- SRC-0044 RA 8293 (Secs. 172, 189, 213)

title: Agriculture and Fishery Arts — organic crop production, aquaculture, animal production and pest management
md:
# HE-A4 — Agriculture and Fishery Arts I and II (exploratory)

Annex F gives this exploratory course **11 items** (Remember 1, Understand 2, Apply 5, Analyze 2, Evaluate 1). Outcomes: **crop production** (organic agriculture, practices, site selection); **aquaculture** (systems, hatchery and nursery, water quality, responsible fish capture); **animal production** (breeds, livestock and poultry management); **pest management** (preventive and corrective measures, organic and conventional protection). [SRC-0002, Annex F, A.4]

## 1. Plain explanation

**Organic agriculture** (RA 10068, amended by RA 11511) grows food without chemical fertilizers, pesticides and drugs, and builds soil fertility, biodiversity and recycling of farm wastes. Products are certified organic by **third-party certification** or a **Participatory Guarantee System (PGS)**.

**Good crop practice** includes **crop rotation** (not monocropping), which cuts pests and weeds and balances soil nutrients; legumes add nitrogen.

**Aquaculture** is raising fish and other aquatic species in fresh, brackish or marine water. In the Philippines the top products are **milkfish (bangus), tilapia, tiger shrimp, seaweed and mud crab**. Systems include **ponds, pens and cages**, bivalve farming on bamboo stakes, and seaweed lines.

**Hatcheries** breed fish and rear larvae; **nurseries** grow the larvae to juveniles (fingerlings) for stocking.

**Responsible fishing** means protecting municipal waters, mangroves, reefs and spawners. The Fisheries Code bans fishing with **explosives, poison or electricity**, **fine-mesh nets**, **muro-ami**, and converting **mangroves** into fishponds.

**Integrated pest management (IPM)** combines cultural, mechanical, biological and chemical controls, and sprays only when pests pass an **action threshold**.

**Animal production** in the Philippines includes the **carabao** (swamp buffalo, draft animal) and poultry raised as **layers** (eggs) or **broilers** (meat), in cages, barns or free-range.

## 2. Testable facts

**Organic agriculture (RA 10068 as amended by RA 11511)**
- **Organic agriculture** includes all systems that promote the ecologically sound, socially acceptable, economically viable and technically feasible production of food and fibers; it **dramatically reduces external inputs by refraining from chemical fertilizers, pesticides and pharmaceuticals**. [SRC-0054, Sec. 3(b)]
- An organic production system aims to **enhance biodiversity**, **increase soil biological activity**, **maintain long-term soil fertility**, **recycle plant and animal wastes** to return nutrients to the land, rely on renewable resources, and minimize pollution of soil, water and air. [SRC-0054, Sec. 3(c)]
- **Conversion period:** the time between the start of organic management and the certification of crops, livestock or aquaculture products as organic. [SRC-0054, Sec. 3(d)]
- Certification types: **first party** (producer sets and checks its own rules), **second party** (buyers or industry set rules), **third party** (an independent body checks compliance). [SRC-0054, Sec. 3(j)–(l)]
- RA 11511 (2020) adds the **Participatory Guarantee System (PGS)**: a locally focused quality-assurance system run by people engaged in organic agriculture, built on trust, social networks and knowledge exchange. [SRC-0055, Sec. 2 amending Sec. 3(s)]
- Products certified by **third-party certification or PGS** may be labelled and sold as **organic**. [SRC-0055, amended Sec. 18]
- The **National Organic Agricultural Board (NOAB)**, attached to the **Department of Agriculture**, is chaired by the **Secretary of Agriculture**. [SRC-0054, Secs. 6–7]

**Crop practices**
- **Crop rotation** grows different crops in sequence on the same land; it reduces dependence on one set of nutrients, pest and weed pressure, and resistant pests. **Monocropping** depletes nutrients and builds specialized pests. [SRC-0162, lead]
- Rotations may aim at weed control, **increasing soil nitrogen** (e.g. with legumes), erosion control or soil structure. [SRC-0162, "Crop choice"]

**Aquaculture**
- **Aquaculture:** fishery operations raising and culturing fish and other species in **fresh, brackish and marine** waters. [SRC-0056, Sec. 4(3)]
- Top five Philippine aquaculture commodities: **milkfish, tilapia, jumbo tiger shrimp, seaweed, mud crab**. Tilapia, carp and catfish are usually freshwater; shrimp and crab brackish; seaweed and green mussel marine; **milkfish grows in fresh, brackish and salt water**. [SRC-0158, "Products farmed"]
- **Fish pens** use the seabed or lakebed as their floor; **fish cages** have an artificial bottom, cost less to build but need more feeding. **Brackish fishponds** are the traditional method, often multi-pond for milkfish. [SRC-0158, "Fish ponds", "Fish pens and cages"]
- Mussels and oysters are grown on **bamboo stakes**; sale is threatened by **red tide**. Seaweed (Eucheuma, Kappaphycus, Caulerpa) is profitable even on small farms; first harvest in about 105–135 days. [SRC-0158, "Bivalves", "Seaweed"]
- Public lands such as tidal swamps, mangroves and foreshore suitable for fishery **may not be disposed of**; a **Fishpond Lease Agreement (FLA)** runs **25 years, renewable for another 25**, primarily for qualified fisherfolk cooperatives. [SRC-0056, Sec. 45]
- Many **mangrove forests** were converted into brackish ponds, often in violation of the law. [SRC-0158, "Land use"]
- In onshore aquaculture, humans control living conditions such as **water quality (oxygen)**, feed and temperature. [SRC-0163, lead]

**Hatchery and nursery**
- A **hatchery** breeds, hatches and rears fish and shellfish through early life stages; juveniles go to on-growing farms. Benefits: **out-of-season supply, genetic improvement, less dependence on wild-caught fry**. [SRC-0159, lead and "Purpose"]
- Steps: **broodstock conditioning** (optimal light, temperature, salinity, flow, food) → **spawning** (natural or induced by stripping, thermal shock or hormone injection) → **fertilization** → **larval rearing in nurseries** to juvenile size. [SRC-0159, "Production steps"]

**Responsible fishing (Fisheries Code RA 8550 as amended by RA 10654; FAO Code)**
- **Municipal waters** extend **15 km** from the coastline; **municipal fishing** uses vessels of **3 gross tons or less** (or no vessel). [SRC-0056, Sec. 4(57)–(58)]
- A **closed season** is a period when taking specified species with specified gear is prohibited in an area. [SRC-0056, Sec. 4(8)]
- Unlawful: fishing with **explosives, noxious or poisonous substances, or electricity**; possession of explosives for illegal fishing. [SRC-0057, Sec. 92]
- Unlawful: nets with **mesh smaller** than DA-set limits (exceptions for gathering fry and similar). [SRC-0057, Sec. 93]
- **Muro-ami** and methods that pound coral reefs are banned; owners and operators face fines of five times the catch value or **₱2 million**, whichever is higher. [SRC-0057, Sec. 97]
- Unlawful to **convert mangroves into fishponds** or for any other purpose. [SRC-0057, Sec. 99]
- Unlawful to catch or possess mature milkfish (**sabalo**) and other breeders/spawners, except for local breeding or research as allowed. [SRC-0057, Sec. 103]
- FAO: **selective and environmentally safe gear** and practices should be developed and given priority, to maintain biodiversity and protect fish quality. [SRC-0111, Art. 6.6]

**Pest management**
- **IPM** (FAO definition): careful consideration of all pest-control techniques, integrating **biological, chemical, physical and cultural** measures to grow healthy crops and **minimize pesticide use** and risks. [SRC-0157, lead]
- First line of defense: **cultural practices** — resistant varieties, healthy crops, crop rotation, intercropping. Then **mechanical** controls: hand-picking, water spraying, barriers, **traps**. [SRC-0157, "Prevention"]
- **Action (economic) threshold:** controls are applied only when pests exceed a level where damage would cost more than treatment; **monitoring** (scouting, traps) is essential. [SRC-0157, "Monitoring"]
- **Biological control** promotes beneficial predators and parasites; **augmentative** biocontrol increases natural enemies. Biopesticides such as **Bt** count as chemical controls. [SRC-0157, "Biological controls", "Chemical controls"]
- IPM's six repeating steps: **sample/monitor → identify → learn pest biology → set action threshold → choose tactics → evaluate**. [SRC-0157, "Process"]
- In Southeast Asian rice, early spraying killed spiders, frogs and wasps that prey on the **brown planthopper** and bred resistance; IRRI encourages planting flowers and vegetables on paddy banks to attract natural enemies. [SRC-0157, "Southeast Asia"]

**Animal production**
- The **carabao** is a genetically distinct **swamp-type water buffalo** of the Philippines, the traditional **draft animal** for paddy rice farming, also used for milk, meat and hide. [SRC-0160, lead and infobox]
- Poultry farming raises chickens, ducks, turkeys and geese for **meat or eggs**; egg-laying hens may be kept **free-range**, in barns, or in **battery cages**; meat chickens (**broilers**) are mostly raised indoors. [SRC-0161, lead and sections]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Organic ≠ "no inputs at all".** Organic farming refrains from *synthetic chemical* fertilizers, pesticides and pharmaceuticals; it uses compost and recycled wastes.
- **PGS vs third-party.** PGS is community-run assurance by practitioners; third-party is an independent certifier. Both allow the "organic" label after RA 11511.
- **Pen vs cage.** A pen uses the natural bottom; a cage has its own net bottom.
- **Hatchery vs nursery.** Hatchery = breeding and hatching; nursery = growing larvae into fingerlings.
- **Municipal waters = 15 km**, not 15 nautical miles; small boats are 3 gross tons or less.
- **IPM does not ban pesticides.** It uses them last, after thresholds are passed.
- **Mangrove conversion is illegal**, even for aquaculture.

## 4. Memory aid

**IPM steps "Some Insects Leave Trails, Catch Early"** = Sample, Identify, Learn biology, Threshold, Choose tactics, Evaluate.
**Top PH aquaculture "Bangus, Tilapia, Sugpo, Seaweed, Alimango."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0054 RA 10068 (Secs. 3, 6–7); SRC-0055 RA 11511
- SRC-0056 RA 8550 (Secs. 4, 45); SRC-0057 RA 10654 (Secs. 92–103); SRC-0111 FAO Code of Conduct Art. 6.6
- SRC-0157 IPM; SRC-0158 Aquaculture in the Philippines; SRC-0159 Fish hatchery; SRC-0160 Carabao; SRC-0161 Poultry farming; SRC-0162 Crop rotation; SRC-0163 Aquaculture — Wikipedia (tertiary; revision ids saved)

title: Common competencies — tools, mensuration, plans and drawings, OSH and work values
md:
# HE-A5 — Common competencies

Annex F gives the exploratory "common competencies" **6 items** (Remember 1, Understand 3, Apply 1, Analyze 1). The outcomes are:
- select, use and maintain tools and equipment;
- perform basic mensuration and calculations;
- read and interpret plans and drawings;
- practice occupational health, safety and ethical values in the workplace;
- apply communication, teamwork, work ethics and problem solving.

[SRC-0002, Annex F, A.5]. These are the skills shared by every TLE area, so TESDA training regulations repeat them across trades.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Safety comes first, by law.** The OSH Standards Act (RA 11058, 2018) makes employers furnish a workplace free of hazards and give safety instructions. It gives workers four rights:
- the right to **know** the hazards;
- the right to **refuse** imminently dangerous work;
- the right to **report** accidents and hazards;
- the right to **free PPE** (personal protective equipment).

Workplaces must post safety signage.

**TESDA's OHS unit** (in Cookery, Housekeeping and other TRs) teaches workers to **identify, evaluate and control** hazards, **maintain awareness** through drills, and **give basic first aid**. Hazards are grouped as **physical, biological, chemical and ergonomic**.

**Mensuration and calculation** means choosing the right measuring tool, measuring accurately, and computing with the four operations, fractions, percentages, unit conversion and area or volume formulas.

**Tool maintenance** means checking condition, setting defective tools aside with labels, doing preventive maintenance, and storing tools properly.

**Technical drawing** means picking the right drawing for the job, reading its dimensions and symbols, and checking it against the job requirements.

## 2. Testable facts

**OSH law (RA 11058)**
- Employers must provide a workplace **free from hazardous conditions**, give **complete job safety instructions or orientation** (especially to new workers), inform workers of hazards and preventive measures, and use only **approved devices and equipment**. [SRC-0063, Sec. 4(a)]
- **Right to know:** workers must be informed of all workplace hazards and given training on chemical, electrical, mechanical and ergonomic safety. [SRC-0063, Sec. 5]
- **Right to refuse unsafe work:** without threat or reprisal, when DOLE determines that an **imminent danger** exists and the employer has not corrected it. [SRC-0063, Sec. 6]
- **Right to report** accidents, dangerous occurrences and hazards to the employer, DOLE and other authorities. [SRC-0063, Sec. 7]
- **Right to PPE:** employers provide protective equipment **free of charge** (eyes, face, hands, feet, lifelines and harnesses, respirators, shields) when the work or environment is hazardous. [SRC-0063, Sec. 8]
- **Safety signage and devices** must be posted prominently, in a language understandable to all, following DOLE standards. [SRC-0063, Sec. 9]
- The cost of an approved safety and health program is **part of operating cost**, and a separate pay item in construction contracts. [SRC-0063, Sec. 20]

**TESDA OHS unit ("Practice occupational health and safety procedures")**
- Elements: (1) identify hazards and risks; (2) evaluate hazards and risks; (3) control hazards and risks; (4) maintain OHS awareness; (5) perform basic first-aid procedures. [SRC-0075, OHS unit]
- Evaluating hazards uses **maximum tolerable limits** based on **threshold limit values (TLV)**. [SRC-0075, OHS unit, element 2.1]
- Hazard types: **physical** (impact, illumination, pressure, noise, vibration, temperature, radiation); **biological** (bacteria, viruses, plants, parasites, mites, molds, fungi, insects); **chemical** (dusts, fibers, mists, fumes, smoke, gases, vapors); **ergonomic** (over-exertion, awkward or static positions, fatigue, monotony, among others). [SRC-0075, OHS unit, range of variables 2]
- **Contingency measures** include evacuation, isolation, decontamination, and calling emergency personnel. [SRC-0075, OHS unit, range of variables 3]
- **PPE** examples: mask, gloves, goggles, hairnet, cap or bonnet, face shield, ear muffs, apron, gown or coverall, anti-static suit. [SRC-0075, OHS unit, range of variables 4]
- **Drills and training** include fire drill, earthquake drill, basic life support or CPR, first aid, spillage control, and disaster preparedness. [SRC-0075, OHS unit, range of variables 5]

**Mensuration and calculation (TESDA "Perform mensurations and calculations")**
- Select measuring instruments: identify the object's **regular geometric shape**, choose tools for the job, and get correct specifications; alternative tools may be used **without sacrificing cost and quality**. [SRC-0084, mensuration unit, element 1]
- Carry out measurements and calculations: obtain accurate measurements; use the **four basic operations**; use **fractions, percentages and mixed numbers**; **self-check** computations for accuracy. [SRC-0084, mensuration unit, element 2]
- Required knowledge: **linear and geometrical measurement**; trade mathematics including **unit conversion, ratio and proportion, and area**; formulas for volume, area and perimeter of plane and solid figures. [SRC-0084, mensuration unit, required knowledge and skills]

**Tools and equipment (TESDA "Maintain tools and equipment")**
- Check condition: identify tools by classification and job; **segregate and label non-functional tools**; observe manufacturers' instructions for tool safety; check the condition of PPE. [SRC-0084, maintain tools unit, element 1]
- Underpinning knowledge includes safety practices (use of PPE, handling of tools, **good housekeeping**) and the types and uses of **lubricants** and **cleaning materials**. [SRC-0084, maintain tools unit, required knowledge]

**Plans and drawings (TESDA "Prepare and interpret technical drawing")**
- Identify the right technical drawing for the job and sort drawings by type. [SRC-0082, technical drawing unit, element 1]
- Interpret: recognize components, identify the **dimensions** of key features, interpret **symbols** correctly, and **check and validate** the drawing against job requirements. [SRC-0082, technical drawing unit, element 2]
- Underpinning knowledge: trade mathematics (linear measurement, dimension, unit conversion), **blueprint reading and plan specification** (architectural, electrical, electronic, mechanical plans; symbols and abbreviations; drawing standards), and **orthographic drawing**. [SRC-0082, technical drawing unit, required knowledge and skills]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Right to refuse is not unconditional.** It applies to an **imminent danger** the employer has not corrected, as determined by DOLE.
- **PPE is free.** The employer pays, not the worker.
- **Hazard categories.** Noise and heat are *physical*; molds and bacteria are *biological*; fumes and dust are *chemical*; awkward posture and repetitive strain are *ergonomic*.
- **Evaluate vs control.** Measuring exposure against TLVs = *evaluate*. Following procedures and using PPE = *control*.
- **Defective tools** are segregated and labeled, not left in the tool box "for later".

## 4. Memory aid

**OHS cycle "I-E-C-M-F"** = Identify, Evaluate, Control, Maintain awareness, First aid.
**Worker rights "Know, No, Tell, Gear"** = right to know, right to refuse, right to report, right to PPE.

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0063 RA 11058 (Secs. 4–9, 20)
- SRC-0075 TESDA Cookery NC II, unit "Practice occupational health and safety procedures"
- SRC-0084 TESDA Plumbing NC II, units "Perform mensurations and calculations" and "Maintain tools and equipment"
- SRC-0082 TESDA Electrical Installation and Maintenance NC III, unit "Prepare and interpret technical drawing"
- SRC-0002 Res. 20 s. 2025, Annex F

title: Entrepreneurship
md:
# HE-A6 — Entrepreneurship

Annex F gives entrepreneurship only **3 items**: Understand, Apply and Analyze, one each [SRC-0002, Annex F, A.6]. Do not over-study it. The outcomes are:
- evaluate business opportunities based on market needs and trends;
- analyze financial statements, manage budgets and assess startup funding;
- apply ethical business practices, **corporate social responsibility (CSR)** and sustainability.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Opportunity.** Not every idea is a business. An idea becomes an **entrepreneurial opportunity** when there is identifiable customer demand *and* it is feasible to meet that demand.

**Money.** A startup reads three core financial statements: the **balance sheet**, the **income statement** and the **statement of cash flows**. The **break-even point** tells how many units must be sold to cover fixed costs.

**Responsibility.** **CSR** means a business sees itself as a member of society with social and environmental obligations, not only a money-maker.

**Philippine forms and laws.**
- Small Home Economics businesses are often sole proprietorships, partnerships, cooperatives or small corporations.
- Philippine law sets the sizes of micro, small and medium enterprises (RA 9501) and gives incentives to barangay micro business enterprises (BMBEs, RA 9178).
- The Cooperative Code defines cooperatives.
- The Revised Corporation Code allows up to 15 incorporators and creates the One Person Corporation.

## 2. Testable facts

- **Entrepreneurial opportunity:** the point where **identifiable consumer demand** meets the **feasibility** of satisfying it. Specific criteria must be met to move from an idea to an opportunity. [SRC-0098, 5.1]
- The three primary financial statements are the **balance sheet, income statement and statement of cash flows**. [SRC-0098, 9.4]
- The statement of cash flows **bridges** the income statement and the balance sheet. Its first section, **operating activities**, covers day-to-day activities such as buying supplies, paying rent and receiving cash from customers. [SRC-0098, 9.4]
- **Contribution margin** = selling price − variable cost per item. [SRC-0098, 9.4]
- **Break-even point (units)** = total fixed costs ÷ contribution margin. Example: price P12, variable cost P4, so the margin is P8; with fixed rent of P2,000, the break-even is 2,000 ÷ 8 = **250 units**. The source uses dollars; the arithmetic is the same. [SRC-0098, 9.4]
- A **business plan** is a formal document for long-range planning, with background, financial information and a summary of the business; investors nearly always ask for one. [SRC-0098, 11.4]
- **CSR**: a business views itself as a member of society with implicit **social obligations and environmental considerations**. Legal compliance and ethical responsibility differ, because the law does not settle every ethical dilemma. [SRC-0098, 3.2]
- **BMBE:** a business entity whose total assets (excluding land) are **not more than P3,000,000**. [SRC-0064, Sec. 3(a)]
- **MSME** asset categories: **micro** not more than P3,000,000; **small** P3,000,001–P15,000,000; **medium** from P15,000,001. MSMEs may be single proprietorships, cooperatives, partnerships or corporations. [SRC-0065, Sec. 3]
- **Cooperative:** an autonomous, duly registered association of persons with a **common bond of interest** who voluntarily join to meet social, economic and cultural needs. Members make equitable capital contributions, patronize its services, and share risks and benefits fairly. [SRC-0066, Art. 3]
- Cooperative principles include **voluntary and open membership** and **democratic member control**, with **one member, one vote** in primary cooperatives. [SRC-0066, Art. 4]
- A corporation may be organized by **not more than 15** incorporators. A **One Person Corporation** is allowed under the Revised Corporation Code. [SRC-0067, Sec. 10]
- A corporation has **perpetual existence** unless its articles of incorporation provide otherwise. [SRC-0067, Sec. 11]
- **Variable costs** rise and fall with how much is made or sold (e.g. ingredients for each pizza). **Fixed costs** such as rent stay the same every month whatever the sales. [SRC-0098, 9.4]
- The **executive summary** gives an overview of the whole business plan; it is best **written last**, even though it comes first in the document. [SRC-0098, 11.4]
- The basic business structures are **sole proprietorships, partnerships and corporations**, plus hybrids; many owners who want **limited liability** form a corporation (or a similar hybrid). [SRC-0098, 13.1]
- The **marketing mix (4 Ps)**: **Product** = the good or service offered; **Price** = what the consumer pays; **Place** = where the product is purchased; **Promotion** = advertising, sales and other communication used to attract customers. [SRC-0099, 1.2]
- An entrepreneurial mindset includes being curious and open, taking **calculated risks**, and being **resourceful and resilient** when facing obstacles; entrepreneurs must **persevere** through challenges. [SRC-0098, 2.1]
- Entrepreneurship takes energy, decision-making skills, **tenacity, resourcefulness and flexibility**. [SRC-0098, 2.3]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Idea ≠ opportunity.** An opportunity needs both demand *and* feasibility.
- **Contribution margin uses variable costs only.** Fixed costs are covered by dividing them by the margin.
- **Cooperative voting** is one member, one vote, not by size of capital.
- **BMBE vs MSME.** BMBE is the P3M-asset category with special incentives under RA 9178. Micro also tops out at P3M under RA 9501. Know which law the question names.
- **CSR is more than legal compliance.**
- **Place is not just a shop.** In the 4 Ps, place means where (and through what channel) the customer buys; advertising belongs to promotion.
- **Fixed costs stay fixed in total**; variable costs follow output.

## 4. Memory aid

**"Break-even = Fixed ÷ (Price − Variable)."**
**"Demand + Doable = Opportunity."**
**4 Ps "What, How much, Where, How they hear": Product, Price, Place, Promotion.**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0098 OpenStax *Entrepreneurship*, 2.1, 2.3, 3.2, 5.1, 9.4, 11.4, 13.1 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
- SRC-0099 OpenStax *Principles of Marketing*, 1.2 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

title: Technology for Teaching and Learning — integrating ed tech, evaluating online resources, gamification and adaptive platforms
md:
# HE-A7 — Technology for Teaching and Learning

Annex F gives this line **3 items** (Understand 1, Apply 1, Analyze 1). Outcomes: integrate educational technology into teaching; **evaluate online resources**, search effectively and manage digital content; use **multimedia, gamification and adaptive platforms** for diverse learners. [SRC-0002, Annex F, A.7] ProfEd B3 (educational technology) overlaps heavily.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Technology changes the teacher's role.** With more computers and internet access, a teacher moves from "full-frontal teaching" to **"guide on the side"**, helping students build their own knowledge. But technology costs money, does not suit every activity, and students need help telling trustworthy sites from "fluff".

**TPACK** says good tech integration blends three kinds of teacher knowledge: **technology (TK), pedagogy (PK) and content (CK)**. The sweet spot where all three overlap is TPACK.

**Evaluate online sources** with the **CRAAP test**: Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose. A faster alternative is **SIFT**: Stop, Investigate the source, Find better coverage, Trace claims to the original.

**Gamification** adds game elements (points, badges, leaderboards, levels, immediate feedback) to ordinary lessons. It is different from **game-based learning**, where students learn by playing or making a game.

**Adaptive learning** uses computer algorithms (and AI) to adjust material and activities to each learner's needs.

**Law still applies.** Copying for classroom teaching can be *fair use* under the IP Code, judged by several factors. Learners' personal data are protected by the Data Privacy Act.

## 2. Testable facts

**Technology and the teacher's role (Seifert & Sutton Ch. 1)**
- Technology has not always been integrated thoroughly, partly because many classrooms have only one or two computers and limited internet; computers then tend to be used in traditional ways (a "fancy typewriter" or encyclopedia). [SRC-0109, Ch. 1 "New trend #2: using technology to support learning"]
- Even one classroom computer can present assignments, enrich students with special interests, and give extra review to those who need it. [SRC-0109, Ch. 1 "New trend #2"]
- More technology makes the shift from **"full-frontal teaching" to "guide on the side"** easier: teachers facilitate students' own construction of knowledge. [SRC-0109, Ch. 1 "New trend #2"]
- Challenges: cost (money taken from staff or books), students needing help to sort **trustworthy information from "fluff"**, and activities (sports, choral practice) that do not suit computers. [SRC-0109, Ch. 1 "New trend #2"]

**TPACK**
- TPACK describes the intersections of **technology, pedagogy and content** for effective technology integration; it builds on **Shulman's pedagogical content knowledge (PCK)**. [SRC-0144, lead and "History"]
- Three base domains: **CK, PK, TK**; pairwise intersections: **PCK, TCK, TPK**; all three together: **TPACK**. Context (XK) surrounds them. [SRC-0144, lead]
- Developed by **Mishra and Koehler** (named TPCK, later TPACK). [SRC-0144, "History"]

**Evaluating online resources**
- **CRAAP = Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose**; created by librarian **Sarah Blakeslee (2004)** to help students judge whether a source is credible. [SRC-0145, lead and "History"]
- Critics prefer step-by-step heuristics such as Mike Caulfield's **SIFT: Stop; Investigate the source; Find better coverage; Trace claims, quotes and media to the original context**. [SRC-0145, "Alternatives and criticisms"]
- Studies found students and even historians are fooled by official-looking **logos and domain names**, while professional fact-checkers reached better-supported conclusions in a fraction of the time. [SRC-0145, "Alternatives and criticisms"]

**Gamification and adaptive platforms**
- **Gamification of learning** uses video-game design and game elements in learning environments to motivate students and keep them participating. [SRC-0146, lead]
- Game elements that can support learning: **points, badges and leaderboards (PBLs)**, narrative and characters, player control, **immediate feedback**, collaborative problem solving, **scaffolded increasing challenge**, mastery and **leveling up**, social connection. [SRC-0146, "Game elements that can facilitate learning"]
- Gamification is **not** game-based learning: in game-based learning students play or create games and the learning is inside the game; **serious games** are built with learning goals in the gameplay. [SRC-0146, lead]
- Surface rewards alone (e.g. badges on a quiz) may raise participation without improving achievement; gamification must be tied meaningfully to learning goals. [SRC-0146, lead]
- **Adaptive learning** uses computer algorithms and artificial intelligence to deliver **customized resources and activities** to each learner's needs; it grew out of **intelligent tutoring** research in the **1970s**. [SRC-0147, lead and "History"]

**Media choice**
- **Edgar Dale** introduced the **Cone of Experience** in **1946** (revised 1954 and 1969) as an intuitive model of how **concrete or abstract** different media are. The popular "we remember 10% of what we read…" percentages are **not Dale's**; he included no numbers. [SRC-0148, "Cone of Experience"]

**Law in the digital classroom**
- **Fair use** for criticism, comment, news reporting, **teaching including multiple copies for classroom use**, scholarship and research is not infringement. Factors include the **purpose and character** of the use (commercial vs non-profit educational) and the **nature of the work**, among others. [SRC-0044, Sec. 185.1]
- Learners' **education and health** records are **sensitive personal information** under the Data Privacy Act. [SRC-0045, Sec. 3(l)]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **TPACK is not "using more gadgets".** It is the fit between content, pedagogy and technology.
- **CRAAP's A's.** Authority = who wrote it; Accuracy = is it supported and correct. Purpose = why it was made (inform, sell, persuade).
- **Gamification ≠ playing games.** Adding badges to a worksheet is gamification; learning fractions through a math adventure game is game-based learning.
- **Dale's Cone has no retention percentages.** An item claiming "Dale found people remember 90% of what they do" is a myth.
- **Fair use is not automatic** for all school copying; it is weighed by factors.

## 4. Memory aid

**"CRAAP before you copy."** Currency, Relevance, Authority, Accuracy, Purpose.
**TPACK "Tech + Teach + Topic."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0109 Seifert & Sutton, *Educational Psychology* 2e (CC BY 3.0), Ch. 1
- SRC-0144 TPACK; SRC-0145 CRAAP test; SRC-0146 Gamification of learning; SRC-0147 Adaptive learning; SRC-0148 Edgar Dale — Wikipedia (tertiary; revision ids saved)
- SRC-0044 RA 8293 Sec. 185; SRC-0045 RA 10173 Sec. 3
- SRC-0002 Res. 20 s. 2025 Annex F

title: Home management — household resources and consumer education
md:
# HE-B1 — Home management: household resources and consumer education

Annex F gives this line **9 items**, mostly *Apply* (5), with *Analyze* (2), *Understand* (1) and *Evaluate* (1). It covers two courses [SRC-0002, Annex F, B.1]:
- **Household resource management:** recognize housekeeping tools, utensils and materials; understand resource-management principles; apply financial management, budgeting and resource allocation; balance household, work and personal life.
- **Consumer education:** interpret consumer **rights and responsibilities**; propose solutions to consumer problems; and evaluate situational problems involving **consumer laws**. That last outcome makes the Consumer Act a must.

## 1. Plain explanation

**The Consumer Act of the Philippines** (RA 7394, 1992) is the main consumer-protection law.
- It protects consumers from unsafe products and from deceptive, unfair or unconscionable sales practices.
- It requires clear labels and price tags and governs warranties.
- It makes manufacturers liable for defective products.
- It orders **consumer education in all schools from primary to secondary level**, which is the legal reason HE teaches it.
- Three departments enforce it, by product type: **DOH** (food, drugs, cosmetics, devices and substances), **DA** (agricultural products) and **DTI** (other consumer products).

**Newer laws** cover new kinds of buying. RA 11967 (2023) protects online shoppers in business-to-consumer and business-to-business transactions. RA 11765 (2022) protects consumers of financial products such as savings, loans and insurance.

**Managing household money** starts with a budget.
- List income and expenses.
- Separate **fixed** expenses (such as rent) from **variable** ones (such as groceries).
- Sort expenses into categories, compare the totals, and plan for the unexpected.
- One simple guideline is **50-30-20**: half to needs, 30% to wants, 20% to savings and debt payments.

**Housekeeping** has a competency standard. TESDA's Housekeeping NC II lists the units a worker must master, from workplace hygiene and safety to cleaning rooms and public areas and doing laundry.

## 2. Testable facts

**Consumer Act (RA 7394): policy and agencies**
- State policy: protect the consumer's interests, promote their general welfare, and set standards of conduct for business and industry. [SRC-0068, Art. 2]
- Objectives: (a) protection against hazards to **health and safety**; (b) protection against **deceptive, unfair and unconscionable** sales acts and practices; (c) **information and education** for sound choices; (d) adequate **rights and means of redress**; (e) involvement of consumer representatives in social and economic policy. [SRC-0068, Art. 2]
- Implementing agencies for product standards: **DOH** for food, drugs, cosmetics, devices and substances; **DA** for agricultural products; **DTI** for other consumer products. [SRC-0068, Art. 6]
- The Act creates a **National Consumer Affairs Council** to improve coordination of consumer programs. [SRC-0068, Art. 148]

**Consumer education and responsibilities**
- The education department, with the Council, must integrate a **consumer education program** into the curricula of **all public and private schools from primary to secondary level**, plus a program for out-of-school youth and adults. [SRC-0068, Art. 154]
- The program teaches four consumer **responsibilities**: **critical awareness** (be alert and questioning about the use, price and quality of goods); **assertiveness** (act to get a fair deal; a passive consumer keeps being exploited); **social concern** (awareness of one's consumption's impact on others, especially the disadvantaged); **environmental awareness** (understand the environmental consequences of consumption and conserve resources for future generations). It also covers **consumer rights** and practical daily problems. [SRC-0068, Art. 154]
- A consumer may file a **petition or letter-complaint** and the concerned department may investigate; departments must set up simple, accessible complaint procedures. [SRC-0068, Art. 159]

**Sales practices, labels, prices**
- A sales act is **deceptive** when the seller, through concealment, false representation or fraudulent manipulation, induces a consumer into a transaction, whether before, during or after it. [SRC-0068, Art. 50]
- A sales act is **unfair or unconscionable** when the seller takes advantage of the consumer's physical or mental infirmity, ignorance, illiteracy, lack of time or surroundings to get a grossly one-sided deal. [SRC-0068, Art. 52]
- **Chain distribution plans or pyramid sales schemes** shall not be used to sell consumer products. [SRC-0068, Art. 53]
- The **metric system** is the official system of weights and measures for products and commercial transactions. [SRC-0068, Art. 63]
- **Minimum label contents** for consumer products: registered trade or brand name; registered trademark; registered business name; Philippine address of the manufacturer, importer or repacker; general make or active ingredients; net quantity in metric units; country of manufacture if imported; among others. [SRC-0068, Art. 77]
- **Price tags:** no consumer product may be offered for retail without a publicly displayed price tag, label or marking. It may not be sold above the tagged price, and the same price applies to all buyers. [SRC-0068, Art. 81]
- **False, deceptive or misleading advertisement** to induce purchases, in any medium, is unlawful. [SRC-0068, Art. 110]

**Warranties and liability**
- A seller or manufacturer giving an **express warranty** must state its terms in clear language: who the warrantor is, who is covered, which products or parts, what the warrantor will do and at whose expense, what the consumer must do, and the period for action. [SRC-0068, Art. 68(a)]
- Written warranties are **operative from the moment of sale**. [SRC-0068, Art. 68(b)]
- Manufacturers, producers and importers are liable **independently of fault** for damages caused by defects in design, manufacture, assembly, formulas, handling, packing, or by inadequate information on use and hazards. A product is **defective** when it does not offer the safety rightfully expected of it. [SRC-0068, Art. 97]

**Online and financial consumers**
- The **Internet Transactions Act** (RA 11967) covers **business-to-business and business-to-consumer** internet transactions under DTI, where a party is in the Philippines or the platform or merchant targets the Philippine market. **Online media content and consumer-to-consumer (C2C)** transactions are **not** covered. [SRC-0069, Sec. 3]
- A **financial consumer** (RA 11765) is a person or entity who buys, leases or receives, or may buy, lease or receive, financial products or services, such as savings and deposits, from a financial service provider. [SRC-0070, Sec. 3(a),(c)]

**Household budgeting**
- **Fixed expenses** do not change over time (rent, car payments, insurance, internet). **Variable expenses** change month to month (gasoline, groceries). [SRC-0090, 6.5]
- Budget steps include **categorizing** expenses, **totaling and comparing** monthly income and expenses (adjust if expenses are higher), and **planning for unplanned expenses**. [SRC-0090, 6.5]
- Yearly, quarterly or semiannual bills are budgeted monthly by **dividing the bill by the number of months it covers**. [SRC-0090, 6.5]
- **50-30-20 budget philosophy:** 50% of income for **needs**, 30% for **wants**, 20% for **savings and debt service**. Wants and needs are often confused. [SRC-0090, 6.5]
- **Simple interest** is computed on the **principal**, the amount borrowed or deposited, using the annual rate and the term in years. [SRC-0090, 6.3]

**Housekeeping competencies (TESDA Housekeeping NC II)**
- Units of competency include: participate in workplace communication; work in team environment; practice career professionalism; practice occupational health and safety; observe workplace hygiene procedures; perform workplace and safety practices; provide effective customer service; provide housekeeping services to guests; clean and prepare rooms for incoming guests; laundry linen and guest clothes; clean public areas, facilities and equipment. [SRC-0078, units of competency]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Rights vs responsibilities.** Article 154's four items (critical awareness, assertiveness, social concern, environmental awareness) are *responsibilities*. "Being alert and questioning about price and quality" = critical awareness. "Speaking up to get a fair deal" = assertiveness.
- **Deceptive vs unfair or unconscionable.** Deceptive = lying or concealing (false representation). Unfair or unconscionable = exploiting a weakness (illiteracy, illness, being rushed) for a grossly one-sided deal.
- **Which agency?** Food, drugs and cosmetics → DOH. Farm products → DA. Most other consumer goods → DTI.
- **Online law scope.** A buy-and-sell between two private individuals (C2C) is **not** covered by RA 11967.
- **Fixed vs variable.** Rent and insurance are fixed even if large; groceries and fuel are variable even if small.
- **Warranty starts at sale**, not at registration or at the first defect.

## 4. Memory aid

**"CASE"** = the four consumer responsibilities in Art. 154: **C**ritical awareness, **A**ssertiveness, **S**ocial concern, **E**nvironmental awareness.
**"50-30-20 = Needs, Wants, Savings."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0068 Consumer Act RA 7394 (Arts. 2, 6, 50, 52, 53, 63, 68, 77, 81, 97, 110, 148, 154, 159)
- SRC-0069 RA 11967 (Sec. 3)
- SRC-0070 RA 11765 (Sec. 3)
- SRC-0090 OpenStax *Contemporary Mathematics*, 6.3 and 6.5 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
- SRC-0078 TESDA Housekeeping NC II
- SRC-0002 Res. 20 s. 2025, Annex F

title: Food science and nutrition
md:
# HE-B2 — Food science and nutrition

Annex F gives this line **12 items** (Understand 2, Apply 6, Analyze 2, Evaluate 1, Create 1). It joins three courses [SRC-0002, Annex F, B.2]:
- **Principles of food preparation:** food selection, preparation and cooking techniques; kitchen tools and equipment; safety and sanitation.
- **Food and nutrition:** nutrients and their roles in the body; planning and preparing nutritious meals for an individual's or family's needs, such as age and budget.
- **Fundamentals of food technology:** food safety and preservation; the chemical makeup of food (carbohydrates, proteins, water, fats, vitamins and minerals) and how it affects quality and safety; microorganisms in food safety and preservation.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Nutrients.** The body needs six classes of nutrients: carbohydrates, lipids (fats), proteins, water, vitamins and minerals.
- The first three are **macronutrients**, needed in large amounts and used for energy.
- Vitamins and minerals are **micronutrients**: needed in small amounts but essential.

**Energy.** Carbohydrates and proteins each give about 4 kilocalories per gram; fats give about 9.

**Vitamins** are either fat-soluble (A, D, E, K) or water-soluble (vitamin C and the B vitamins).

**Deficiencies.** Too little of a vitamin or mineral causes a typical deficiency disease, such as scurvy, rickets, beriberi, pellagra, anemia or goiter. Severe lack of protein causes kwashiorkor; lack of both protein and calories causes marasmus.

**Food safety.** It rests on four habits: **clean, separate, cook, chill**. Keep hot food hot and cold food cold. Food can be contaminated by bacteria, viruses, parasites, and toxins from molds.

**Preservation** methods, old and new, keep food safe and protect its flavor, color, moisture and nutrients.

**In the Philippines:**
- The *Nutritional Guidelines for Filipinos* (NGF, revised 2012) give the official messages.
- *Pinggang Pinoy*, the healthy food plate for adults, **completes** the daily nutritional guide pyramid; it did not replace it.
- Laws require iodized salt (ASIN law), food fortification, and a food safety regulatory system.

## 2. Testable facts

**Nutrients and energy**
- **Six classes of nutrients:** carbohydrates, lipids, proteins, water, vitamins and minerals. [SRC-0108, ch. 1 Introduction]
- **Macronutrients** (needed in large amounts) are carbohydrates, lipids and proteins; they can be processed into cellular energy. [SRC-0108, ch. 1 Introduction]
- **Micronutrients** (needed in lesser amounts) are all the essential minerals and vitamins: **16 essential minerals** and **13 vitamins**. [SRC-0108, ch. 1 Introduction]
- Energy: carbohydrates **4 kcal/g**, proteins **4 kcal/g**, lipids **9 kcal/g**. [SRC-0108, ch. 1 Introduction]
- Lipids also form cell membranes, protect organs, and insulate the body for temperature regulation. [SRC-0108, ch. 1 Introduction]
- Providing energy is not protein's most important job. Proteins build the structure of bones, muscles and skin and run most of the body's chemical reactions. [SRC-0108, ch. 1 Introduction]

**Vitamins**
- The 13 vitamins are **water-soluble** (vitamin C and all the B vitamins: thiamine, riboflavin, niacin, pantothenic acid, pyridoxine, biotin, folate, cobalamin) or **fat-soluble** (**A, D, E, K**). [SRC-0108, ch. 1 Introduction]
- Vitamin C is not stored in significant amounts. The higher the intake, the more is excreted. [SRC-0108, ch. 10 Water-Soluble Vitamins]
- **Vitamin A deficiency:** **night blindness** is its most definitive sign. Severe deficiency causes **xerophthalmia** (dry eyes, Bitot's spots), which can progress to corneal ulceration and blindness. [SRC-0108, ch. 9 Fat-Soluble Vitamins]
- **Vitamin D deficiency:** **rickets** in children (soft, weak, deformed bones); **osteomalacia** in adults. [SRC-0108, ch. 9 Fat-Soluble Vitamins]
- **Vitamin C deficiency: scurvy.** Signs include bleeding gums, skin disorders, painful joints, weakness, depression and more infections. Vitamin C is essential for making **collagen**. [SRC-0108, ch. 10 Water-Soluble Vitamins]
- **Thiamin (B1) deficiency: beriberi.** Symptoms include fatigue, confusion, movement problems, leg pain, swelling and heart failure. It is common where the staple is **white rice**, because milling removes the bran. [SRC-0108, ch. 10 Water-Soluble Vitamins]
- **Niacin (B3) deficiency: pellagra.** It starts with fatigue, poor appetite and indigestion, then the **four D's: diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and sometimes death**. [SRC-0108, ch. 10 Water-Soluble Vitamins]

**Minerals**
- **Iron:** low iron reduces the oxygen-carrying capacity of red blood cells, causing **anemia**. [SRC-0108, ch. 11 Iron]
- **Iodine** is essential for making **thyroid hormone**, which regulates basal metabolism, growth and development. Iodine prevents **goiter**, a gross enlargement of the thyroid gland in the neck. [SRC-0108, ch. 11 Iodine]

**Protein deficiency**
- **Kwashiorkor** is caused by severe dietary **protein** deficiency. Signs: **edema** (swelling of feet and abdomen, a pot-belly), poor skin, growth retardation, low muscle mass, liver malfunction, and light-colored thinning hair. The edema occurs because too little protein means too little albumin to hold water in the blood vessels. [SRC-0108, ch. 6 Diseases Involving Proteins]
- The name kwashiorkor comes from a language in Ghana, meaning "rejected one". It is common in children recently weaned and fed low-protein grain porridge. [SRC-0108, ch. 6 Diseases Involving Proteins]
- **Marasmus**: neither enough **protein nor enough calories**. Signs: extreme **emaciation**, poor skin, growth retardation. It mostly affects children under one in poor countries; the name is Greek for "starvation". [SRC-0108, ch. 6 Diseases Involving Proteins]

**Food safety and microorganisms**
- The **four steps** for safe food handling: **Clean** (wash hands, surfaces, utensils, produce); **Separate** (avoid cross-contamination, e.g. separate cutting boards for produce and for meat, poultry, seafood and eggs); **Cook** (heat to proper temperatures, checked with a food thermometer); **Chill** (refrigerate leftovers within **two hours**). [SRC-0108, ch. 17 Efforts on the Consumer Level]
- Hot food should be kept above **140°F**; cold food at **40°F (4°C) or lower**. The refrigerator should be kept at 40°F (4°C) or colder. [SRC-0108, ch. 17 Efforts on the Consumer Level]
- Store raw meat at the **bottom** of the refrigerator so juices do not drip onto other foods. Keep eggs on a shelf, not in the door, where it is warmest. [SRC-0108, ch. 17 Efforts on the Consumer Level]
- Foodborne illnesses are **infections** (caused by microbes such as bacteria) or **intoxications** (caused by toxins, such as those produced by molds). [SRC-0108, ch. 17 Major Types of Foodborne Illness]
- **Salmonella**, found in the intestines of birds, reptiles and mammals, spreads through meats, poultry, eggs, dairy and seafood. Salmonellosis brings fever, diarrhea and cramps within **12–72 hours**. [SRC-0108, ch. 17 Causes of Food Contamination]
- **Molds** are microscopic fungi that grow in warm, humid or damp conditions on many foods. [SRC-0108, ch. 17 Causes of Food Contamination]
- Proteins give food structure and texture; cooking **denatures** proteins and changes their functional qualities. [SRC-0108, ch. 6 Role of Proteins in Foods]

**Food preservation**
- Traditional methods: **curing, smoking, pickling, salting, fermenting, canning**, and preserving fruit as jam. Modern methods: **drying, vacuum packing, pasteurization, freezing and refrigeration**. Preservation guards against foodborne illness and protects flavor, color, moisture and nutritive value. [SRC-0108, ch. 17 Food Preservation]

**Philippine guidelines and laws**
- **Fortification** means adding nutrients to processed foods at levels **above their natural state**. A **micronutrient** is an essential nutrient needed in very small quantities (milligrams or micrograms). [SRC-0061, Sec. 3(c),(e)]
- The **ASIN law** (RA 8172) makes salt fortification a priority health program. All food outlets, restaurants and stores must make **only iodized salt** available to customers. [SRC-0060, Secs. 2, 5(c)]
- The **Food Safety Act** (RA 10611) aims to protect the public from food-borne and water-borne illness and from unsanitary, unwholesome, misbranded or adulterated food. [SRC-0058, Sec. 3(a)]

**Cooking methods and preparation terms (Stage 7 addition; Wikipedia, tertiary, because no open culinary text was reachable)**
- **Sauté:** cook in a **small amount of fat** in a shallow pan over **relatively high heat**; the name means "jumped" (tossing). [SRC-0239, lead]
- **Blanch:** scald briefly in **boiling water**, then plunge into **iced or cold water** ("shocking") to stop cooking. [SRC-0240, lead]
- **Braise:** a **combination** method: brown at high temperature first, then **simmer covered** in liquid. [SRC-0241, lead]
- **Poach:** heat food **submerged in liquid** at a **lower** temperature than simmering or boiling, about **70–80 °C**. [SRC-0242, lead]
- **Broil:** grilling with the heat source **above** the food (US term). [SRC-0243, lead]
- **Deep-fry:** food **submerged in hot fat**, unlike shallow (pan) frying. [SRC-0244, lead]
- **Steam:** cook with **steam**; the food sits in the steam, not in the water. [SRC-0248, lead]
- **Marinate:** soak food in a **seasoned, often acidic** liquid (the marinade) before cooking. [SRC-0249, lead]
- **Julienne:** long, thin **matchstick** strips. **Dice:** small **cubes**, uniform for even cooking. **Mince:** **small, uniform pieces**, finer than dice. [SRC-0245, lead; SRC-0247, lead; SRC-0246, lead]
- **Temperature danger zone:** the range in which food-borne bacteria grow readily; agencies define it differently, roughly **4 to 63 °C**. Keep hot foods hot and cold foods cold. [SRC-0253, lead]
- **Kneading** works bread dough to mix it and give strength by forming **gluten**. **Creaming** butter and sugar beats **air bubbles** into the fat, giving a light, fluffy mixture. A **sieve** (sifter) separates lumps and controls particle size. [SRC-0250, lead; SRC-0252, Baking; SRC-0251, lead]

- **Roasting** cooks with **dry heat**, hot air surrounding the food (at least about 150 °C). **Whisking or whipping** beats **air** into a mixture such as cream or egg whites. [SRC-0269, lead; SRC-0268, lead]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Pellagra has four D's** in our source (diarrhea, dermatitis, dementia, and death), not just three. If an option lists only three, it can still be the best answer, but know all four.
- **Kwashiorkor vs marasmus.** Swelling or a pot-belly despite eating = kwashiorkor (protein). Extreme thinness, "skin and bones" = marasmus (protein *and* calories).
- **Pinggang Pinoy did not replace the pyramid**. It completes it.
- **Iodine is a mineral, not a vitamin**. Iron (anemia) and iodine (goiter) are minerals.
- **Fat-soluble is "A, D, E, K"**. Vitamin C and the B vitamins are water-soluble.
- **Fat has more than double the energy per gram** (9) of carbohydrate or protein (4 each).
- **Infection vs intoxication.** Live microbes = infection; toxins (e.g. from molds) = intoxication.
- **Poach vs boil vs simmer.** Poaching is the *gentlest* (about 70–80 °C). Braising starts dry (browning) and ends wet.
- **Broil vs grill.** In broiling the heat comes from **above**.
- **Julienne = strips, dice = cubes, mince = finest.**

## 4. Memory aid

**"A Dog Eats Kibble"** = fat-soluble A, D, E, K.
**"4-4-9"** = carbohydrate, protein, fat kcal per gram.
**"Clean, Separate, Cook, Chill — and Chill within 2."**
**"Strips, Cubes, Crumbs"** = julienne, dice, mince. **"Brown then Bathe"** = braise.

## 5. Sources
