title: Food service management — school food service, safe handling, storage, service and the national feeding program
md:
# HE-B3 — Food service management (school food service)

Annex F gives this line **6 items** (Understand 1, Apply 3, Analyze 1, Evaluate 1). Outcome: **school food service** — preparing, managing and serving in the school cafeteria, and caring for and safely using tools, supplies and equipment. [SRC-0002, Annex F, B.3]

A school canteen is a **food establishment** under the Code on Sanitation, a **food business** under the Food Safety Act (with the **LGU** responsible for school canteens), and the site of the **school-based feeding program** under RA 11037. HE-B7 covers sanitary permits, health certificates and food-handler dress; this lesson covers washing, sanitizing, storage, service, and the feeding program.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Dishwashing has three stages:** scrape and pre-rinse; wash in warm soapy water; then **sanitize** (hot water, chlorine, steam or hot air). Air-dry on racks instead of wiping with cloths. Store cups and glasses **upside down**, off the lowest shelves.

**Storage:** dry goods in covered containers on shelves in a cool room; perishables in the refrigerator at **7 °C or below**, each kind at its own range.

**Serving:** do not touch food or the eating surfaces of utensils; serve with tools, not fingers; keep clean and soiled linens apart.

**Service styles:** American (plate), Russian (platter), buffet. A cafeteria is a self-service line.

**Feeding program (RA 11037):** DepEd gives at least **one fortified meal** a day for at least **120 days** a year to undernourished public school children from kindergarten to Grade 6.

## 2. Testable facts

**Washing and sanitizing utensils (PD 856)**
- Equipment and utensils must be easy to clean and safe; **lead-soldered containers and cadmium-lined piping** must not be used; food-contact surfaces must be impervious, corrosion-resistant, non-toxic, easy to clean, durable and chip-resistant. [SRC-0059, Sec. 23]
- Washing: **scrape and pre-rinse**; wash thoroughly in **warm water at 49 °C (120 °F)** with soap or detergent; change wash water often if running water is not used. [SRC-0059, Sec. 24]
- Bactericidal treatment after washing, one of: immersion **at least 30 seconds in water at 77 °C (170 °F)** or more; immersion **at least 1 minute in lukewarm 50 ppm chlorine** solution; steam cabinet; or oven/hot-air cabinet **at 82 °C (180 °F) for at least 20 minutes**; or another method approved by the local health authority. [SRC-0059, Sec. 25]
- Washed utensils **drain-dry on wire racks without drying cloths**, or are stored self-draining for air-drying. [SRC-0059, Sec. 26(a)]
- Store utensils in a clean, dry place protected from vermin; **cups, bowls and glasses are inverted**; utensils are not stored on the **bottom shelves** of open cabinets below the working top. [SRC-0059, Sec. 27]

**Storage (PD 856)**
- Dry, non-perishable foods: designated spaces and shelves; containers of **metal with tight covers**; recommended dry-store temperature about **10–15 °C**. [SRC-0059, Sec. 28]
- Perishable foods are kept **at or below 7 °C (45 °F)** except during preparation or when held for immediate serving. [SRC-0059, Sec. 29(a)]
- Recommended ranges: **meat and fish 0–3 °C**; **milk and milk products 5–7 °C**; **fruits and vegetables 7–10 °C** (stored in cool rooms). [SRC-0059, Sec. 29(c)–(d)]
- Refrigerators must be clean, in good repair, odor-free, have **thermometers**, and enough shelving to avoid overstocking and allow ventilation. [SRC-0059, Sec. 29(e)]

**Food service hygiene (PD 856)**
- **Avoid hand contact** with food; fingers are not used to serve butter, ice and similar items; sugar is served in covered dispensers or single-service packets. [SRC-0059, Sec. 30(a)]
- The surfaces of glasses and tableware that touch food or the mouth are **not handled**; single-service items are stored in sanitary cartons and handled without touching the food-contact surface. [SRC-0059, Sec. 30(b)–(c)]
- Clean linens are stored in designated clean places; **soiled linens go into a closed, marked bin**. [SRC-0059, Sec. 30(d)]
- Dippers and scoops for frozen desserts are kept in **running water** or water at 77 °C, or washed and dried after each use. [SRC-0059, Sec. 30(e)]

**Food service operations (TESDA Food and Beverage Services NC II)**
- Serving styles: **American (plate) service**, **Russian (platter) service**, **buffet** service. [SRC-0077, "Provide food and beverage services", range of variables 1]
- Sequence of service: greet → seat → take beverage orders → present menu → take food orders → (wine) → serve food → crumb the table → coffee/tea → present the bill. [SRC-0077, "Provide food and beverage services", range of variables 2]
- The **"3-minute check"** confirms guest satisfaction soon after serving (replenish condiments, add items, clear unused items). [SRC-0077, "Provide food and beverage services", element 2.5 and range of variables 3]
- Closing down: remove soiled dishes, handle **food scraps per hygiene rules**, clean and store equipment, reset tables, **turn off electrical equipment**. [SRC-0077, "Provide food and beverage services", element 6]
- Preparing the dining area includes stocking service stations, cleaning and placing tableware, filling water pitchers, and **wiping the necks and tops of condiment bottles**. [SRC-0077, "Prepare the dining room/restaurant area", element 2]

**Food Safety Act (RA 10611)**
- **Food business operators** must ensure food meets food-law requirements and that controls prevent, eliminate or reduce risks to consumers. [SRC-0058, Sec. 13]
- If an operator believes a food is unsafe, it must **immediately withdraw it** and inform authorities; if it may have reached consumers, inform them and **recall** it. [SRC-0058, Sec. 14(b), (d)]
- **LGUs** are responsible for food safety in food businesses such as wet markets, restaurants, catering, water refilling stations and **school canteens**; DA covers primary production; DOH covers processed and prepackaged foods. [SRC-0058, Sec. 15]

**School feeding (RA 11037, Masustansyang Pagkain para sa Batang Pilipino Act, 2018)**
- **DepEd** runs the **school-based feeding program** for undernourished public school children from **kindergarten to Grade 6**; **DSWD** runs supplemental feeding in day care centers for children **3 to 5**. [SRC-0062, Secs. 3(d), 4(a)–(b)]
- Each gives **at least one fortified meal** for **not less than 120 days** a year. [SRC-0062, Sec. 4(a)–(b)]
- A **fortified meal** supplies at least **one-third of the daily requirement** based on the PDRI. **Cycle menus** are standardized by the NNC and FNRI and adapted to age, location and local or religious food preferences. [SRC-0062, Sec. 3(a)–(b)]
- Other components: milk feeding with locally produced fresh milk, micronutrient supplements and **iodized salt**, deworming and health exams, **Gulayan sa Paaralan** school gardens, **WASH** facilities, and nutrition education. [SRC-0062, Sec. 4(c)–(h)]

**HACCP and the danger zone (Stage 7 addition; Wikipedia, tertiary)**
- **HACCP** = **Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Points**: a **systematic, preventive** approach to food safety covering **biological, chemical and physical** hazards in production. [SRC-0254, lead]
- By 1997 **seven HACCP principles** became the standard. [SRC-0254, Principles]
- The **danger zone** is the temperature range where food-borne bacteria grow readily, roughly **4–63 °C** depending on the agency; potentially hazardous food should not be stored in it. [SRC-0253, lead]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Wash ≠ sanitize.** Soap and warm water clean; the 77 °C dip, chlorine, steam or hot air sanitizes.
- **Do not towel-dry** sanitized dishes; air-dry on racks.
- **Glasses go upside down**, not right side up "to keep them ready".
- **Perishables ≤ 7 °C.** Milk 5–7 °C, meat and fish colder (0–3 °C).
- **DepEd vs DSWD.** DepEd: K–6 school feeding. DSWD: day care, ages 3–5.
- **Who checks school canteens for food safety?** The LGU, under RA 10611.
- **"One-third"**: a fortified meal gives at least one-third of the daily requirement, not the full day.
- **HACCP is preventive**, not end-product testing only.

## 4. Memory aid

**Dishwashing "Scrape, Scrub, Sanitize, Stand to dry."**
**RA 11037 "1-120-⅓"**: one fortified meal, 120 days, one-third of daily needs.
**"HACCP: Hunt hazards, Control at Critical Points."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0059 PD 856 (Secs. 23–30)
- SRC-0058 RA 10611 (Secs. 13–15)
- SRC-0062 RA 11037 (Secs. 3–4)
- SRC-0077 TESDA Food and Beverage Services NC II
- SRC-0002 Res. 20 s. 2025 Annex F
- SRC-0253, SRC-0254 Wikipedia: Danger zone (food safety); HACCP (CC BY-SA 4.0)

title: Family life and child development
md:
# HE-B4 — Family life and child development

Annex F gives this line **15 items**, the most of any Home Economics line. Most are *Apply* items (7), with *Understand* (3), *Analyze* (3) and *Evaluate* (2). The outcomes are:
- differentiate developmental milestones from infancy to adolescence, and apply child development theories
- use healthy communication, conflict resolution and emotional intelligence in marriage and family
- apply parenting styles
- analyze family structures, roles and dynamics
- assess cultural, social and economic factors in Filipino families

[SRC-0002, Annex F, B.4]. The major development theories (Piaget, Erikson, Vygotsky, Kohlberg, Bronfenbrenner) are in the PE-C1 lesson. Learn them there and apply them here.

## 1. Plain explanation

**The legal family.** In the Philippines, marriage and family relations are governed by the **Family Code** (Executive Order No. 209, 1987).
- It calls marriage a special contract of permanent union and the foundation of the family.
- A valid marriage needs essential requisites (legal capacity and freely given consent) and formal requisites (an authorized solemnizing officer, a marriage license, and a ceremony with witnesses).
- If any requisite is missing, the marriage is void from the beginning. Some defects make a marriage only voidable.
- Both parents share parental authority over their children.

**Family forms.** Sociology describes families by structure and by how a person enters them.
- **Nuclear family:** parents and children.
- **Extended family:** a household that also includes other relatives, such as grandparents, aunts and cousins.
- **Single-parent and blended families** are common variations.
- **Family of orientation:** the family you are born into.
- **Family of procreation:** the family formed through marriage.

**The family over time.** The *family life cycle* describes predictable stages, from a childless couple, through children of different ages, to launching and the "empty nest".

**Parenting styles.** Diana Baumrind's styles vary by **warmth** and **structure**. A fourth style, uninvolved, was added later by Maccoby and Martin.

**Before birth.** Prenatal development has three periods: germinal, embryonic and fetal. Organ formation happens in the embryonic period, and harmful substances (teratogens) can disrupt development.

**Protecting family members.** RA 7610 protects children, RA 9262 protects women and their children from violence in intimate and family relationships, and RA 10354 (the RH Law) defines adolescents as ages 10–19.

## 2. Testable facts

**Marriage under the Family Code (EO 209)**
- Marriage is "a special contract of permanent union between a man and a woman", entered into according to law to establish conjugal and family life; it is the foundation of the family. [SRC-0071, Art. 1]
- **Essential requisites:** (1) legal capacity of the contracting parties, who must be a male and a female; (2) **consent freely given** in the presence of the solemnizing officer. [SRC-0071, Art. 2]
- **Formal requisites:** (1) authority of the solemnizing officer; (2) a valid **marriage license**, except in cases the Code exempts; (3) a marriage ceremony with the parties appearing before the officer and declaring they take each other as spouses, before **at least two witnesses of legal age**. [SRC-0071, Art. 3]
- Absence of any essential or formal requisite makes the marriage **void ab initio** (void from the beginning), except as stated in Art. 35(2). [SRC-0071, Art. 4]
- Minimum age to marry: **18**. [SRC-0071, Art. 5]
- **Void** marriages include those where a party is **below 18**, even with parental consent; those solemnized by an unauthorized person (with a good-faith exception); those without a license (unless exempt); bigamous or polygamous marriages; and those contracted through mistake about the other party's identity. [SRC-0071, Art. 35]
- A marriage is also void if a party was **psychologically incapacitated** to fulfil the essential marital obligations, even if this shows only after the wedding. [SRC-0071, Art. 36]
- A marriage is **voidable** (may be annulled) for causes existing at the time of marriage. An example: a party aged **18 to below 21** married without parental consent, unless they freely cohabited after turning 21. [SRC-0071, Art. 45]
- **Parental authority:** the father and the mother **jointly** exercise it over their common children; in disagreement the father's decision prevails unless a court orders otherwise. [SRC-0071, Art. 211]
- Parents are **civilly liable** for injuries and damages caused by their unemancipated children living with them, subject to the defenses allowed by law. [SRC-0071, Art. 221]

**Family forms and the family life cycle**
- **Extended family:** a household with at least one parent and child plus other relatives such as grandparents, aunts, uncles and cousins. [SRC-0088, 14.1]
- **Family of orientation:** the family a person is born into. **Family of procreation:** the family formed through marriage. [SRC-0088, 14.1]
- **Monogamy:** married to one person at a time. **Polygamy:** married to more than one at a time. [SRC-0088, 14.1]
- The **functionalist** view: families perform vital roles inside the family and for society. They provide for members' physical, emotional and social well-being; parents care for and socialize children; adult children often later care for elderly parents. [SRC-0088, 14.1]
- Single-parent families, blended families, foster families and cohabitation are variations sociology studies alongside the two-parent family. [SRC-0088, 14.2]
- The **family life cycle** idea began with **Paul Glick (1955)**: people grow up, form families, rear and launch children, experience an empty nest, and the cycle repeats. [SRC-0088, 14.1]
- **Evelyn Duvall's** classic stages: (1) marriage family, childless; (2) procreation family, children 0–2.5; (3) preschooler family, 2.5–6; (4) school-age family, 6–13; (5) teenage family, 13–20; (6) launching family, children begin to leave; (7) empty nest family. [SRC-0088, 14.1 Table 14.1]
- Each life-cycle stage has its own structure and challenges, and family success can be judged by how well the family adapts to each transition. [SRC-0088, 14.1]

**Parenting styles**
- **Diana Baumrind** identified three parenting styles that differ in **warmth** and **structure** (strictness). [SRC-0087, 6.3]
- **Authoritarian:** high structure (rules, boundaries, discipline), **low warmth**; rules-focused; directs and demands rather than negotiates. [SRC-0087, 6.3]
- **Authoritative:** moderate to high structure **and high warmth** and emotional support; relationship-focused; talks things through; more democratic and less rigid than authoritarian. [SRC-0087, 6.3]
- **Permissive:** **high warmth, low structure**; child-focused; avoids discipline and gives in to requests. [SRC-0087, 6.3]
- **Uninvolved:** **low structure, low warmth**; little attention, discipline or support; parent-focused. This fourth style was added by **Maccoby and Martin (1983)**, not Baumrind. [SRC-0087, 6.3]

**Prenatal development**
- Three periods of pregnancy: **germinal, embryonic, fetal**. [SRC-0087, 2.3]
- **Germinal:** the first and shortest, from conception to about **two weeks**. The zygote divides within 24 hours, becomes a **blastocyst** about 5–7 days later, and implants in the uterus. [SRC-0087, 2.3]
- **Embryonic:** from the **third to the eighth week**. The amnion, chorion, placenta and umbilical cord form, and **organogenesis** (organ formation) takes place. [SRC-0087, 2.3]
- **Fetal:** the last **seven months**, a period of organ growth and refinement in which the fetus grows quickly. [SRC-0087, 2.3]
- A teratogen's impact depends on the specific agent, the length and amount of exposure, genetic susceptibility, and the prenatal environment. Different body features have different sensitive periods. [SRC-0087, 2.3]

**Laws that protect family members**
- **Adolescent:** young people aged **10 to 19**, in transition from childhood to adulthood (RH Law). [SRC-0072, Sec. 4(b)]
- **Children** under RA 7610: persons **below 18**, or older but unable to protect themselves because of a disability or condition. [SRC-0029, Sec. 3(a)]
- **VAWC** includes physical, sexual and psychological harm and **economic abuse** by a husband, former husband, or partner in a dating or sexual relationship or with a common child. It covers the woman and her child. [SRC-0028, Sec. 3(a)]
- The Early Years Act treats ages **0 to 8** as the first crucial stage of educational development. [SRC-0074, title]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Essential vs formal requisites.** Essential = *who* and *consent* (legal capacity; consent freely given). Formal = *procedure* (officer's authority, license, ceremony with two witnesses). A missing license is a *formal* defect.
- **Void vs voidable.** Under 18 = void, even with parental consent. Ages 18–20 without parental consent = voidable (annullable). Psychological incapacity = void (Art. 36), not voidable.
- **Authoritarian vs authoritative.** Both have structure. Only *authoritative* adds high warmth. "Because I said so" with little warmth = authoritarian.
- **Uninvolved was not Baumrind's.** Baumrind had three styles; Maccoby and Martin added the fourth.
- **Prenatal weeks.** Germinal ≈ 0–2 weeks; embryonic = weeks 3–8; fetal = the rest (about seven months). Do not put organ formation in the fetal period; the fetal period *grows and refines* organs.
- **Adolescent age range.** The RH Law says 10–19. The Family Code minimum marriage age is 18. RA 7610's "child" is below 18. They answer different questions.
- **Family life cycle names differ by author.** Duvall's stages are one classic version. Exam items usually test the *order* (couple → young children → school age → teens → launching → empty nest).

## 4. Memory aid

**"License, Officer, Witnesses = Form; Capacity + Consent = Essence"**: the 3 formal and 2 essential requisites of marriage.
**Parenting grid "Warmth × Rules"**: high-high = Authoritative; low warmth + high rules = Authoritarian; high warmth + low rules = Permissive; low-low = Uninvolved.
**Prenatal "2-8-7"**: germinal ≈ 2 weeks, embryonic to week 8, fetal ≈ 7 months.

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0071 Family Code, EO 209 (Arts. 1–5, 35, 36, 45, 211, 221)
- SRC-0088 OpenStax *Introduction to Sociology 3e*, 14.1–14.2 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
- SRC-0087 OpenStax *Lifespan Development*, 2.3 and 6.3 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
- SRC-0072 RA 10354 (Sec. 4)
- SRC-0029 RA 7610 (Sec. 3)
- SRC-0028 RA 9262 (Sec. 3)
- SRC-0074 RA 10410
- SRC-0002 Res. 20 s. 2025, Annex F

# HE-B5 — Arts and crafts

Annex F gives this line **12 items** (Understand 2, Apply 6, Analyze 2, Evaluate 1, Create 1). Outcomes: art forms in **daily life and cultural identity**; applying art and creativity to everyday life (living spaces, **DIY crafts**); the role of **handicraft industries in culture and economy**; the **history of Philippine handicraft**; **famous handicrafts of selected regions**. [SRC-0002, Annex F, B.5] GE-06 (Art Appreciation) shares the art-elements material.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Crafts are culture you can use.** Mats, baskets, woven cloth, carved wood and metalwork are both **useful** and **expressive**. They carry each community's identity: T'boli t'nalak, Ilocano inabel, Maranao okir, Paete woodcarving.

**The State protects them.** The **Manlilikha ng Bayan Act (RA 7355, 1992)** honors master folk artists who keep a tradition alive and teach it. The **National Cultural Heritage Act (RA 10066)** protects cultural property, including **intangible heritage** such as traditional craftsmanship. The **Tropical Fabrics Law (RA 9242)** creates demand for local fibers.

**Crafts are also livelihood.** RA 7355 itself calls for vocational courses based on an awardee's methods and for studying how to turn the art into a **cottage industry**. Piña, abacá, banig and capiz products are traded nationally and abroad.

**Design still matters.** DIY crafts and home decoration use the elements of design (line, shape, color, texture, value, form, space), color schemes, and compositional techniques such as the rule of thirds.

## 2. Testable facts

**GAMABA — Manlilikha ng Bayan Act (RA 7355, 1992)**
- **Manlilikha ng Bayan:** a citizen or group engaged in a traditional art uniquely Filipino whose skills have reached a high level of technical and artistic excellence and have been **passed on to and widely practiced** by the present generation in the community. [SRC-0048, Sec. 3]
- **Traditional folk art:** expressions of distinctiveness and artistic quality serving **decorative, utilitarian or sociocultural** functions. [SRC-0048, Sec. 3]
- Criteria: (a) **technical and creative skill** (mastery of tools and materials); (b) **artistic quality**; (c) **community tradition** (has transferred or will transfer the skill); (d) **folk art tradition in existence and documented for at least 50 years**; (e) **character and integrity**. [SRC-0048, Sec. 4]
- Incentives: plaque or medal (duplicate displayed in the provincial museum); **₱100,000 initial grant and ₱10,000 a month for life**; documentation of works; possible **vocational course** based on the awardee's methods; DTI feasibility study to turn the art into a **cottage industry**. [SRC-0048, Sec. 5]
- The award is implemented by the **National Commission for Culture and the Arts (NCCA)**, following UNESCO's Living Human Treasures concept; it replaced the 1988–1992 National Folk Artists Award. [SRC-0170, "History"]
- Categories include **weaving, carving, pottery, textile or fiber arts, ornament, folk architecture, maritime transport, performing arts, literature, graphic and plastic arts**; **ethnomedicine** was added in 2020. [SRC-0170, "Categories"]

**GAMABA awardees in crafts (selected)**
- **Lang Dulay** (T'boli, Lake Sebu, South Cotabato, 1998): **t'nalak** abaca-ikat weaving. [SRC-0170, "Recipients"]
- **Salinta Monon** (Tagabawa-Bagobo, Davao del Sur, 1998): abaca-ikat (inabal) weaving. [SRC-0170, "Recipients"]
- **Darhata Sawabi** (Tausug, Sulu, 2004): **pis syabit** weaving. **Haja Amina Appi** (Sama, Tawi-Tawi, 2004): master **mat** weaver. **Eduardo Mutuc** (Kapampangan, Apalit, Pampanga, 2004): **pinukpuk** bronze and silver metalwork. [SRC-0170, "Recipients"]
- **Magdalena Gamayo** (Ilocano, Pinili, Ilocos Norte, 2012): **inabel/abel** weaving. **Teofilo Garcia** (San Quintin, Abra, 2012): **tabungaw** native headgear. [SRC-0170, "Recipients"]
- **Ambalang Ausalin** (Yakan, Lamitan, Basilan, 2016): Yakan **tennun** tapestry weaving. [SRC-0170, "Recipients"]
- **Ginaw Bilog** (Hanunuo Mangyan, Oriental Mindoro, 1993) preserved the **Mangyan script and poetry (ambahan)** written on bamboo. [SRC-0170, "Recipients"]

**Cultural heritage law (RA 10066)**
- **Cultural property:** all products of human creativity by which a people and nation reveal their identity, **movable or immovable, tangible or intangible**. [SRC-0049, Sec. 3(o)]
- **Intangible cultural heritage** includes oral traditions, performing arts, rituals and festive events, knowledge about nature, and **traditional craftsmanship**. [SRC-0049, Sec. 3(x)]
- **National Cultural Treasure:** a unique cultural property of outstanding value, **officially declared** by the pertinent cultural agency; **Important Cultural Property** has exceptional significance as determined by the National Museum and/or NHI. [SRC-0049, Sec. 3(w), (bb)]
- The **NCCA** is "the Commission" under the Act; cultural agencies include the **National Museum, National Library, NHI, National Archives, CCP, and KWF**. [SRC-0049, Sec. 3(h)–(j)]

**Famous regional crafts**
- **T'nalak:** T'boli (South Cotabato) cloth of **abacá**, resist-dyed by **ikat**, woven on a **backstrap loom** by women who receive designs **in dreams** ("dreamweavers"); designs are a gift from **Fu Dalu**, goddess of abacá. [SRC-0171, lead]
- **Inabel (abel):** Ilocano handwoven **cotton** textile from the **Ilocos Region and Abra**, woven on **hardwood pedal looms**; the **binakul** (whirlwind) pattern is said to ward off evil spirits. [SRC-0172, lead and "Description"]
- **Piña:** pineapple-leaf fiber woven into sheer **nipis**; **Aklan** piña handloom weaving is on UNESCO's intangible heritage list (2023). **Abacá** (Manila hemp) is endemic to the Philippines; the country produces most of the world's supply. [SRC-0142, lead; SRC-0143, lead]
- **Banig:** handwoven mats, typically of **pandan or sedge** (also buri, reed, rattan); the Waray of **Basey, Samar** weave banig from **tikog**. [SRC-0173, lead and "Regional/ethnic styles"]
- **Okir (okil):** curvilinear and rectilinear plant-based motifs of the **Maranao** and other Moro groups; decorates the **torogan** (royal house) with carved **panolong** beams; motifs include the **naga** (S-shaped sea serpent). [SRC-0174, lead and "History"]
- **Paete, Laguna:** "**Carving Capital of the Philippines**", known for woodcarving (ukit) and **taka** (papier-mâché formed over carved wooden molds). [SRC-0175, lead and "Taka"]
- **Capiz shell:** shell of the windowpane oyster (*Placuna placenta*), long used as a **glass substitute** in windows and for decorative items. [SRC-0176, lead]

**Design for everyday crafts**
- Elements of design: **line, shape, color, texture, value, form, space**. [SRC-0155, "Elements of design"]
- Compositional techniques include the **rule of thirds**, rule of odds, rule of space, simplification, geometry and symmetry, and creating movement. [SRC-0155, "Compositional techniques"]
- Color schemes: monochromatic, analogous, complementary, split-complementary, triadic. [SRC-0153, scheme sections]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **GAMABA ≠ National Artist.** GAMABA (RA 7355) honors *traditional folk* artists of a community; the Order of National Artists honors other artists.
- **50 years** is the minimum age of the *tradition*, not of the artist.
- **T'nalak is abacá, inabel is cotton.** T'nalak = T'boli, South Cotabato; inabel = Ilocano, Ilocos/Abra.
- **Okir is a motif tradition (Maranao)**, not a fabric.
- **Paete = woodcarving and taka**, not pottery.
- **Intangible heritage includes craftsmanship skills**, not only songs and dances.

## 4. Memory aid

**GAMABA criteria "Skill, Art, Teach, 50 years, Character" (SAT-5-C).**
**Regional crafts map: "Ilocos abel, Laguna carves, Aklan piña, Samar banig, South Cotabato t'nalak, Lanao okir."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0048 RA 7355 (Secs. 3–5); SRC-0049 RA 10066 (Sec. 3); SRC-0050 RA 9242
- SRC-0170 Gawad sa Manlilikha ng Bayan; SRC-0171 T'nalak; SRC-0172 Inabel; SRC-0173 Banig; SRC-0174 Okir; SRC-0175 Paete; SRC-0176 Capiz shell; SRC-0142 Piña; SRC-0143 Abacá; SRC-0153 Color scheme; SRC-0154 Elements of art; SRC-0155 Composition — Wikipedia (tertiary; revision ids saved)

title: Clothing construction and design — selection and care, body measurement, pattern drafting, sewing tools and construction

# HE-B6 — Clothing construction and design

Annex F gives this line **12 items** (Understand 2, Apply 6, Analyze 2, Evaluate 1, Create 1). Outcomes: **clothing selection, purchase and care**; **principles of clothing construction**; sewing **materials, tools and equipment**; **body measurement**; **pattern drafting**. [SRC-0002, Annex F, B.6] Expect scenario items: which measurement, which tool, which grain, what a care symbol means, what went wrong with a seam.

HE-A2 covers fibers, Philippine fabrics and the four machine faults; HE-B8 covers machine types and maintenance. This lesson goes deeper on measuring, drafting, cutting, sewing and care.

## 1. Plain explanation

**The TESDA dressmaking sequence** is: plan the design with the client → take body measurements in order → draft a basic (block) pattern → manipulate it into the style → cut the final pattern → prepare and cut fabric → sew → apply finishing touches → press.

**A block pattern (sloper)** is a basic, fitted pattern (bodice, skirt, trousers) from which many styles are made. Patterns are drafted flat from measurements, or made by **draping** fabric on a form.

**Grain matters.** Straight grain runs along the selvedge (warp threads) and stretches least, so most garments are cut with it running top to bottom. **Bias** (45°) stretches most and drapes softly.

**Seam allowance** is the strip between the cut edge and the stitching line. Patterns are cut with or without it.

**Selection and care.** Choose design and fabric for the client and the occasion. Follow care labels: washing tub, bleach triangle, dryer square, iron dots, professional-cleaning circle.

**Design.** Clothes use the same elements as art: line, shape, color, texture, value, form, space. Color schemes (monochromatic, analogous, complementary, triadic) guide combinations.

## 2. Testable facts

**Body measurement and pattern drafting (TESDA Dressmaking NC II, "Draft and cut pattern for casual apparel")**
- Elements: (1) plan garment design; (2) take client's body measurements; (3) draft basic/block pattern; (4) manipulate pattern; (5) cut final pattern. [SRC-0080, draft and cut pattern unit]
- Design and **fabric are discussed and selected** according to the client's specifications, and the client's **special needs** (pocket, stitch, collar, sleeve, skirt, cut) are incorporated. [SRC-0080, draft and cut pattern unit, element 1 and range of variables 3]
- Measurements are taken **in sequence**, following standard body measurement, and **recorded**. Assessors check the **correct position and sequence** of measuring. [SRC-0080, draft and cut pattern unit, element 2 and evidence guide 1.4]
- Standard body measurements listed: shoulder; neck circumference; chest width and bust circumference; bust height and width; figure (front and back); **waistline; hips**; lengths of sleeve, blouse, skirt and dress; **armhole circumference**. [SRC-0080, draft and cut pattern unit, range of variables 5]
- Measuring tools: **tape measure, hip curve rule, L-square, meter stick**. [SRC-0080, draft and cut pattern unit, range of variables 4]
- Drafting tools: **tailor's chalk, pattern paper, ruler with grid, triangle (45°–90°), hip curve, French curve, pencil**. Cutting tool: **scissors**. [SRC-0080, draft and cut pattern unit, range of variables 6, 8]
- Basic/block patterns listed: blouse, skirt, trouser, shorts, culottes, shirt. Final pattern is **labeled**, filed and secured; it is cut **with or without seam allowance**. [SRC-0080, draft and cut pattern unit, elements 4–5 and range of variables 7, 9]
- A **sloper (block) pattern** is a custom-fitted basic pattern from which many styles are developed; changing the size of a finished pattern is **grading**. [SRC-0151, lead]
- Pattern symbols: **notches** mark seam allowances, centerlines, zipper placement and matching points; **circular holes** mark dart apex, pocket and buttonhole placement; a **long arrow is the grainline**, placed parallel to the straight grain; **double lines** show where to lengthen or shorten. [SRC-0151, "Standard pattern symbols"]
- **Flat-pattern method:** pattern drafted on a flat surface from measurements with rulers and curves. **Draping:** pinning fabric (e.g. calico) on a form to make a mock-up pattern. [SRC-0151, "Pattern making"]

**Preparing and cutting fabric**
- Fabric is checked for **quality, faults, width and selvedges**, soaked or drip-dried and pressed; patterns are pinned **along the grain line** and seam allowances marked before cutting. [SRC-0080, "Prepare and cut materials", elements 1–2]
- Underpinning knowledge: **fabric properties such as weight, shrinkage, pile, grain and pattern shapes**. [SRC-0080, "Prepare and cut materials", evidence guide 2.2]
- **Straight grain** runs parallel to the warp threads and **selvedge** and has the **least stretch**; most garments are cut with it running top to bottom. [SRC-0150, "Straight grain"]
- **Cross grain** runs perpendicular to the selvedge, along the weft, with more stretch. [SRC-0150, "Cross grain"]
- **Bias** is any direction between them; **true bias is 45°**. Woven fabric is most elastic and fluid on the bias, so bias-cut garments drape and cling to body curves. [SRC-0150, "Bias"]
- **Seam allowance** is the area between the fabric edge and the stitching line. Home-sewing patterns use **1/4 to 5/8 inch** (about 6–16 mm); 5/8 in (1.5 cm) is common and helps with fabrics that ravel. Curved areas (neckline, armhole) get narrower allowances. [SRC-0149, lead]

**Sewing and finishing (Dressmaking NC II)**
- Accessories and accents: **zipper, buttons, bias tape, hook and eye**. [SRC-0080, "Prepare and cut materials", range of variables 4]
- Sleeve types listed: **puff, tailored, cup**. [SRC-0080, "Sew casual apparel", range of variables 3]
- In finishing, bodice **hem allowances** and sleeves are folded and pinned, and **hemline allowances are sewn** per the given stitch/seam specifications. [SRC-0080, "Apply finishing touches", elements 1.6–1.7]
- Faults to correct before release: **grease/oil spots, puckering, loose threads, missing buttons, uneven stitches**. [SRC-0080, "Apply finishing touches", range of variables 3]

**Care labels**
- A **care label** carries pictograms for washing, bleaching, drying, ironing and professional cleaning. [SRC-0152, lead]
- **Wash tub**: the number is the maximum water temperature in °C (US labels use dots). **Triangle**: bleach allowed; two oblique lines = no chlorine bleach; crossed = **no bleach**. **Square with circle**: tumble dryer. **Iron** with 1, 2 or 3 dots = about **110, 150, 200 °C**. **Circle**: professional (dry) cleaning. [SRC-0152, "Washing", "Bleaching", "Drying", "Ironing", "Professional cleaning"]

**Design and color**
- Elements of design: **line, shape, form, color, space, texture, value**. Color has three properties: **hue, intensity (chroma), value**. [SRC-0154, sections "Line" to "Value"]
- Color schemes: **monochromatic** (tints and shades of one hue), **analogous** (neighbors on the color wheel), **complementary** (opposites; maximum contrast), **split-complementary** (a base plus the two colors beside its complement), **triadic** (three evenly spaced hues, 120° apart). [SRC-0153, "Monochromatic", "Complementary", "Analogous", "Evenly spaced hues"]

**Philippine context**
- Government uniforms must use **Philippine tropical fabrics** (natural fibers produced, spun, woven or knitted and finished in the Philippines). [SRC-0050, Secs. 2–3]

**Shaping, fullness and finishing terms (Stage 7 addition; Wikipedia, tertiary)**
- **Darts** are folds that taper to a point, sewn to take in ease and **give shape** to a garment, especially at the bust. [SRC-0258, lead]
- **Gathering** turns an edge into many **small, irregular folds** held by a thread near the edge; the fabric becomes shorter where stitched and flares beyond. [SRC-0259, lead]
- A **pleat** is a fold made by **doubling fabric back on itself and securing it**; pleats are structured, unlike soft gathers. [SRC-0260, lead]
- A **hem** is an edge **folded and sewn** to **prevent unravelling** and set the length, as at the bottom of a garment or sleeve end. [SRC-0263, lead]
- A **seam ripper** is a small tool for **cutting and removing stitches**; its forked head has a cutting edge at the base of the fork. [SRC-0261, lead]
- A **tracing wheel** has teeth on a wheel and **transfers pattern markings onto fabric**, with or without tracing (carbon) paper. [SRC-0262, lead]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Draft before cut, block before style.** The block is drafted from measurements first, then manipulated into the final pattern.
- **Straight grain = along the selvedge**, not across it. Bias is diagonal (45°), not "the edge".
- **Hip curve vs French curve.** Both are curves; the hip curve is for long gentle curves (hip, side seam), the French curve for tighter ones (neck, armhole). (General tailoring knowledge; TESDA lists both tools.)
- **Crossed triangle = no bleach**, not "no washing". The circle alone is dry or professional cleaning, not tumble drying (that is a circle *inside a square*).
- **More iron dots = hotter.** Silk (Level 1) gets the coolest iron; cotton and linen higher.
- **Complementary ≠ analogous.** Opposite on the wheel vs side by side.
- **Dart vs pleat vs gather.** Dart = pointed fold for *fit*; pleat = pressed, structured fold; gather = soft, irregular bunching from pulled thread.

## 4. Memory aid

**Dressmaking flow "Plan–Measure–Draft–Style–Cut–Sew–Finish–Press."**
**Care symbols "Tub, Triangle, Square, Iron, Circle" = Wash, Bleach, Dry, Press, Pro-clean.**
**"Dart = Do-fit; Pleat = Pressed; Gather = Gentle bunch."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0080 TESDA Dressmaking NC II (draft and cut pattern; prepare and cut materials; sew casual apparel; apply finishing touches)
- SRC-0149 Seam allowance; SRC-0150 Grain (textile); SRC-0151 Pattern (sewing); SRC-0152 Laundry symbol; SRC-0153 Color scheme; SRC-0154 Elements of art — Wikipedia (tertiary; revision ids saved)
- SRC-0050 RA 9242
- SRC-0002 Res. 20 s. 2025 Annex F
- SRC-0258–SRC-0263 Wikipedia: Dart (sewing), Gather (sewing), Pleat, Seam ripper, Tracing wheel, Hem (CC BY-SA 4.0)

title: Workplace safety, occupational health standards and ethical practices in Home Economics

# HE-B7 — Workplace safety, occupational health standards and ethics in HE

Annex F gives this line **5 items** (Understand 2, Apply 2, Analyze 1). [SRC-0002, Annex F, B.7] Items are likely to be situations in an HE workplace: a kitchen, a canteen, a salon, a sewing room.

HE-A5 already covers the four OSH worker rights (know, refuse, report, PPE) and TESDA's hazard types. This lesson adds **how a workplace organizes safety** (program, committee, safety officer, training, welfare facilities, penalties), the **Sanitation Code rules for food workers**, **salon safety**, and **professional ethics**.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Organizing safety (RA 11058).** Every covered workplace needs a written **OSH program**, an **OSH committee**, a **safety officer**, health personnel, training, and basic welfare facilities. The employer pays for all of this as part of normal operating costs. Employers who ignore OSH standards face daily fines.

**Food workers (PD 856, Sanitation Code).** A food establishment needs a **sanitary permit** from the local health office, posted where people can see it. Every worker needs a **health certificate**. Food handlers wear clean clothes and caps or hairnets, keep good hygiene, and wash and dry hands before work and after using the toilet.

**Salons (TESDA Beauty Care).** Keep walkways clear, remove spills and hair promptly, disinfect linen, store and check tools, rotate stock, and lift safely.

**Ethics and professionalism (TESDA "Practice career professionalism").** Align personal goals with the organization's, prioritize work, use resources economically, keep learning, and keep licenses and certificates current.

## 2. Testable facts

**OSH program, committee and officer (RA 11058)**
- Covered workplaces must have a **safety and health program** that includes, among others: a commitment to comply; a **drug-free workplace**; HIV/AIDS, tuberculosis and hepatitis prevention; PPE; safety signage; **toolbox meetings**; accident investigation and reporting; an **emergency preparedness and response plan**; and waste management. [SRC-0063, Sec. 12]
- The program is prepared by the employer **in consultation with workers**, submitted to **DOLE**, and made available to everyone in the workplace. [SRC-0063, Sec. 12]
- The **OSH committee**: the **employer or representative is chairperson**; the **safety officer is secretary**; members include contractor safety officers, health personnel (ex officio) and **workers' representatives** (from the union, or elected by simple majority if there is no union). [SRC-0063, Sec. 13]
- A **safety officer** is trained by DOLE and tasked to implement the program. Duties: oversee the program, monitor and inspect, assist government inspectors, and **issue work stoppage orders when necessary**. [SRC-0063, Secs. 3(n), 14]
- All workers must take the mandatory **eight-hour safety and health seminar** required by DOLE. [SRC-0063, Sec. 16(b)]
- Welfare facilities required: safe **drinking water**, sanitary and washing facilities, living quarters where applicable, and **separate** sanitary, washing and sleeping facilities for men and women where applicable. [SRC-0063, Sec. 19]
- The employer, project owner, contractor and anyone who manages or supervises the work are **jointly and solidarily liable** for compliance. [SRC-0063, Sec. 21]
- If work stops because of an imminent danger caused by the **employer's** violation, the employer **pays the workers' wages** during the stoppage. [SRC-0063, Sec. 23]
- Willful non-compliance: administrative fine **not exceeding ₱100,000 per day** until corrected, counted from notice of the violation. Retaliating against workers who gave information to inspectors carries an added ₱100,000 fine. [SRC-0063, Sec. 28(a)–(b)]

**Food establishments (PD 856, Code on Sanitation)**
- No food establishment may operate for public patronage without a **sanitary permit** from the local health office; the permit is **posted in a conspicuous place**. A "food establishment" is where food or drinks are manufactured, processed, stored, sold or served. [SRC-0059, Sec. 14(a)–(b)]
- After a change of owner or occupant, the new occupant must have the change **noted within 14 days**. [SRC-0059, Sec. 14(d)]
- No person may be employed in a food establishment without a **health certificate** from the local health authority, issued after physical and medical exams and required immunizations. [SRC-0059, Secs. 15, 19(a)]
- Food handlers must wear **clean working garments**; the **cook wears a prescribed cap**, and female employees wear caps or **hairnets**; they observe good personal hygiene. [SRC-0059, Sec. 19(b)]
- Food handlers wash hands with **soap and water** and dry them with a clean or disposable towel or hand dryer **immediately before working and after visiting the toilet**. [SRC-0059, Sec. 19(b)(iii)]

**Kitchen OHS (TESDA Cookery NC II)**
- The Cookery TR's OHS unit lists required emergency-related drills: fire drill, earthquake drill, basic life support/CPR, first aid, spillage control, disaster preparedness. [SRC-0075, OHS unit, range of variables 5]
- Safety regulations listed in the OHS unit include the Clean Air Act, the Building Code, the **National Electrical and Fire Safety Codes**, waste-management rules and the Philippine OSH Standards. [SRC-0075, OHS unit, range of variables 1 (safety regulations)]

**Salon safety (TESDA Beauty Care NC II, "Maintain a safe, clean and efficient work environment")**
- Comply with health regulations: apply salon policies on **personal hygiene** and follow state and local **health regulations**. [SRC-0079, safe work environment unit, element 1]
- Keep reception, work areas and **walkways uncluttered**; store and dispose of waste per OHS requirements; **promptly remove spills, hair and other hazards** from floors; store, clean and **disinfect linen**. [SRC-0079, safe work environment unit, element 2]
- Store tools safely, prepare them for each service, check maintenance needs and **refer for repair**; carry out **stock rotation** and record stock levels; use **safe lifting and carrying** techniques. [SRC-0079, safe work environment unit, elements 3–4]

**Professional ethics (TESDA "Practice career professionalism")**
- Elements: (1) integrate personal objectives with organizational goals; (2) set and meet work priorities; (3) maintain professional growth and development. [SRC-0075, career professionalism unit]
- Setting priorities includes using resources **efficiently** and following practices on the **economic use and maintenance of equipment and facilities**. [SRC-0075, career professionalism unit, element 2]
- Professional growth includes obtaining and **renewing licenses and certifications** (e.g. National Certificates, Certificates of Competency, professional licenses). [SRC-0075, career professionalism unit, element 3 and range of variables 5]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Chair vs secretary.** The *employer* chairs the OSH committee; the *safety officer* is secretary.
- **Who pays?** OSH program costs and PPE are the employer's; wages during an imminent-danger stoppage caused by the employer are paid.
- **Sanitary permit vs health certificate.** The *establishment* gets a sanitary permit (posted); each *worker* gets a health certificate.
- **Hairnets and caps** are a Sanitation Code requirement, not just a "best practice".
- **Safety officers can stop work.** That is an explicit duty.
- **Ethics in TESDA terms** is about goals, priorities, economical use of resources and keeping certifications, not only "honesty".

## 4. Memory aid

**"Permit on the wall, certificate in the wallet."** (Sanitary permit is posted; health certificate is personal.)
**OSH committee "Boss chairs, Officer writes, Workers sit."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0063 RA 11058 (Secs. 3, 12–16, 19, 21, 23, 28)
- SRC-0059 PD 856 (Secs. 14, 15, 19)
- SRC-0075 TESDA Cookery NC II (OHS unit; career professionalism unit)
- SRC-0079 TESDA Beauty Care NC II (safe, clean and efficient work environment unit)
- SRC-0002 Res. 20 s. 2025 Annex F

title: Appropriate tools, equipment, materials and technology in Home Economics
md:
# HE-B8 — Appropriate tools, equipment, materials and technology in HE

Annex F gives this line **4 items** (Understand 2, Apply 2). [SRC-0002, Annex F, B.8] Expect "which tool or material fits this task" and "what to do with a faulty tool" questions.

The TESDA training regulations for HE trades list the tools and materials each trade uses. This lesson collects the ones most likely to be tested: kitchen cleaning, baking, sewing and housekeeping. General tool maintenance (segregate and label defective tools) is in HE-A5.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Match the tool to the job and the material.** Cleaning agents are chosen for the surface (glass, wood, steel, carpet). Baking equipment is chosen for the product (mixers, scales, pans, moulds). Sewing tools are chosen for the step (measure, cut, sew, press).

**Keep tools clean and working.** Kitchen equipment is cleaned and sanitized with potable water and the right chemicals, then stored safely. Sewing machines are cleaned and lubricated as the manufacturer says. Faults are reported, not hidden.

**Measure accurately.** Bakers **weigh** and measure ingredients by recipe; dressmakers use tape measures and rulers made for curves and right angles.

**Use protective clothing** when handling cleaning chemicals.

## 2. Testable facts

**Kitchen cleaning (TESDA Cookery NC II, "Clean and maintain kitchen premises")**
- Elements: (1) clean, sanitize and store equipment; (2) clean and sanitize premises; (3) dispose of waste. [SRC-0075, clean and maintain kitchen premises unit]
- Equipment and utensils are cleaned and sanitized with **chemicals and clean potable water**, following **manufacturer's instructions**, then stored or stacked safely in the designated place. [SRC-0075, kitchen premises unit, element 1]
- Premises are cleaned on a **cleaning schedule**; walls, floors, shelves and working surfaces are cleaned without damage to health or property; **first aid** procedures are followed if an accident happens. [SRC-0075, kitchen premises unit, element 2]
- Wastes are **sorted** and disposed of per sanitary regulations; cleaning **chemicals are disposed of safely**. [SRC-0075, kitchen premises unit, element 3]
- Cleaning equipment and supplies listed: **chemical dispensers**; paper towels, cleaning agents and **sanitizers**. [SRC-0075, kitchen premises unit, range of variables 3]
- Required knowledge includes **environment-friendly** cleaning products and practices, and **cross-contamination** issues. [SRC-0075, kitchen premises unit, evidence guide 2]

**Baking (TESDA Bread and Pastry Production NC II, "Prepare and produce bakery products")**
- Ingredients are **selected, measured and weighed** according to the recipe; the **oven temperature** is chosen for the desired product characteristics. [SRC-0076, bakery products unit, elements 1.1, 1.5]
- Baking equipment: commercial **mixers and attachments**, cutting implements, **scales**, measures, bowls, **ovens**, moulds, shapes and cutters, baking sheets and pans. [SRC-0076, bakery products unit, range of variables 4]
- Bread-baking techniques: beating, whisking, **folding**, rolling, **laminating**, **creaming**, **kneading**, incorporating fat, make-up and **proofing**; plus scaling, panning and baking. [SRC-0076, bakery products unit, range of variables 5]
- Bakery product types: **lean-yeast dough** (crisp- and soft-crusted breads, rye/whole wheat, sourdough), **soft dough** (loaves and buns), **rich-yeast dough** (sweet dough, rolled-in/laminated dough), **quick breads** (muffins, shortcakes), doughnuts and pancakes, cookies. [SRC-0076, bakery products unit, range of variables 2]
- Product quality is judged by **color, consistency and texture, moisture, mouth feel, appearance**. [SRC-0076, bakery products unit, range of variables 3]
- Storage considers **temperature, light and air exposure**, proper containers, **labeling**, display cabinets and refrigeration or freezing time. [SRC-0076, bakery products unit, range of variables 9]

**Sewing (TESDA Dressmaking NC II)**
- Machine types: **single-needle lockstitch**, double-needle lockstitch, **edging** machine, **buttonhole** machine. [SRC-0080, "Set up and operate machine", range of variables 1]
- Basic machine maintenance: operate and monitor the machine; **clean and lubricate** it per the manufacturer's instructions; check operation and **document and report** problems to the supervisor. [SRC-0080, "Perform basic maintenance", elements 1–3]
- **Minor** machine faults: loose threads, broken needle, machine control. **Major** faults: electric motor defect, **timing not synchronized**, broken body parts. [SRC-0080, "Perform basic maintenance", range of variables]
- Measuring tools for pattern drafting: **tape measure, hip curve rule, L-square, meter stick**. [SRC-0080, "Draft and cut pattern", range of variables 4]

**Housekeeping (TESDA Housekeeping NC II, "Clean public areas, facilities and equipment")**
- Select equipment for the type of cleaning; check it is clean and safe **before use**; choose **dry and wet cleaning agents** per the manufacturer and OSH rules; wear **protective clothing** where needed. [SRC-0078, clean public areas unit, element 1]
- Cleaning equipment and chemicals are chosen according to the **type of material** being cleaned: glass, leather, fabrics, brass/steel, wood, carpet, hard floors. [SRC-0078, clean public areas unit, element 2 and range of variables 3]
- Protective clothing: overalls, jackets, aprons, **goggles and masks**, waterproof clothing and footwear, headwear. [SRC-0078, clean public areas unit, range of variables 2]
- Hazards to watch for include spills, **wet or slippery surfaces**, fumes, blood, **needles and syringes**, broken glass, sharp objects, and hot utensils and surfaces. [SRC-0078, clean public areas unit, range of variables 5]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Weigh, don't guess** in baking. The TR says ingredients are *measured and weighed*.
- **Lean vs rich dough.** Lean-yeast dough makes crusty breads and sourdough; rich-yeast dough (with more fat and sugar) makes sweet and laminated doughs. Muffins are *quick* breads (no yeast).
- **Minor vs major sewing-machine faults.** A broken needle is minor; a motor defect or out-of-time hook is major and goes to a technician.
- **Same chemical for every surface** is wrong; choose by material.
- **Cleaning chemicals are not poured anywhere**; they are disposed of by standard procedure.

## 4. Memory aid

**"Right tool, right material, right care, report the fault."**
**Bread techniques "B-W-F-R-L-C-K-P"**: Beat, Whisk, Fold, Roll, Laminate, Cream, Knead, Proof — "Bakers Will Fold Rolls Lovingly, Cream, Knead, Proof."

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0076 TESDA Bread and Pastry Production NC II ("Prepare and produce bakery products")
- SRC-0080 TESDA Dressmaking NC II (machine set-up, basic maintenance, pattern drafting)
- SRC-0078 TESDA Housekeeping NC II ("Clean public areas, facilities and equipment")

title: Assessment in Home Economics — competency-based assessment, authentic and performance assessment, rubrics, portfolios, using data
