title: The teacher and the school curriculum — planning, design, development and evaluation
md:
# PE-B1 — The teacher and the school curriculum

Section B of ProfEd is **45 items** (30%). Our working split gives this line about **15 items**. Outcomes: curriculum **planning, design, development and evaluation**. [SRC-0001, Annex A, ProfEd B]

## 1. Plain explanation

**What is a curriculum?** The planned set of goals, content, learning experiences and assessments a school offers. Students also learn a **hidden curriculum** — norms and values no one openly set out to teach.

**Classic planning model: Tyler (1949).** Four questions: purposes → learning experiences → organization → evaluation.

**Backward design: Understanding by Design (Wiggins & McTighe, 1998).** Start from desired results, then decide on evidence (assessment), then plan activities.

**Spiral curriculum (Bruner).** Revisit topics at increasing depth. K to 12 is required by law to use the **spiral progression approach**.

**Philippine curriculum law (RA 10533).** K to 12 = 1 year kindergarten + 6 elementary + 4 junior high + 2 senior high. The curriculum must be learner-centered, inclusive, developmentally appropriate, relevant, research-based, culture-sensitive, contextualized and global, constructivist and inquiry-based, spiral, and flexible enough to **localize and indigenize**. RA 12027 (2024) discontinued the mother tongue as medium of instruction in K–3.

**From standards to lessons.** Standards (broad) → curriculum framework (scope and sequence, specific skills) → curriculum guide → unit and lesson objectives.

**Writing objectives.** Mager's behavioral objectives: observable behavior, condition, and criterion. Bloom's taxonomy sorts objectives by thinking level.

## 2. Testable facts

**Curriculum models**
- **Ralph Tyler**, *Basic Principles of Curriculum and Instruction* (**1949**): (1) What **educational purposes** should the school seek to attain? (2) How can **learning experiences** be selected? (3) How can they be **organized**? (4) How can their effectiveness be **evaluated**? [SRC-0177, "Thoughts on curriculum"]
- Tyler: "It is what he does that he learns, not what the teacher does." He headed evaluation for the **Eight-Year Study** (1933–1941) and is called the father of educational evaluation. [SRC-0177, lead, "Eight-Year Study", "Thoughts on curriculum"]
- **Understanding by Design** (Wiggins & McTighe, 1998) is **backward design**: Stage 1 identify **desired results** (understandings, essential questions); Stage 2 determine **assessment evidence**; Stage 3 plan **learning activities**. [SRC-0178, lead and "Backward design"]
- Backward design responds to the habit of starting planning with **activities and textbooks** instead of goals. [SRC-0178, "Backward design"]
- **Spiral curriculum (Jerome Bruner):** each subject is revisited at intervals at a **more sophisticated level** each time, linking later learning to earlier learning. [SRC-0180, lead]
- **Hidden curriculum:** lessons "which are learned but not openly intended", such as norms, values and beliefs conveyed in the classroom and social environment; it can reinforce social inequalities. [SRC-0181, lead]

**K to 12 law (RA 10533, Enhanced Basic Education Act of 2013)**
- Structure: at least **1 year kindergarten, 6 years elementary, 6 years secondary** (**4 junior high + 2 senior high**). Kindergarten entrants are at least **5 years old**; typical entrant ages are **6** (Grade 1), **12** (JHS) and **16** (SHS). [SRC-0021, Sec. 4]
- **DepEd** formulates the curriculum, working with **CHED** (harmonized basic and tertiary curricula) and **TESDA**, and consulting DOLE, PRC, schools, teachers, parents and industry. [SRC-0021, Sec. 5]
- Curriculum standards and principles: (a) **learner-centered, inclusive, developmentally appropriate**; (b) **relevant, responsive, research-based**; (c) **culture-sensitive**; (d) **contextualized and global**; (e) pedagogy that is **constructivist, inquiry-based, reflective, collaborative and integrative**; (f) MTB-MLE principles ("from the known to the unknown"); (g) **spiral progression**; (h) **flexible** so schools can **localize, indigenize and enhance** it. [SRC-0021, Sec. 5(a)–(h)]
- Approval of locally produced teaching materials **devolves to regional and division** offices. [SRC-0021, Sec. 5(h)]
- A **Curriculum Consultative Committee** chaired by the DepEd Secretary (with CHED, TESDA, DOLE, PRC, DOST and business representatives) oversees review and evaluation of the curriculum. [SRC-0021, Sec. 6]
- **RA 12027 (2024)** **discontinued** the mother tongue as **medium of instruction** in kindergarten to Grade 3; instruction reverts to **Filipino and English**, with regional languages as **auxiliary** media. [SRC-0022, Sec. 1]
- MTB-MLE may still be used in **monolingual classes** that meet requirements (KWF orthography, documented vocabulary, materials, trained teachers); DepEd and KWF develop a **language mapping** policy. [SRC-0022, Sec. 2]

**From standards to classroom objectives (Seifert & Sutton Ch. 10)**
- **Standards** statements are general; a **curriculum framework** organizes standards into specific skills (the **scope and sequence**) and names observable behaviors; a **curriculum guide** is more detailed still. Neither standards nor frameworks lay out daily activity plans. [SRC-0109, Ch. 10 "Curriculum frameworks and curriculum guides"]
- Two approaches to objectives: the **cognitive** approach moves from **general to specific** (goals with representative **indicators**, Gronlund); the **behavioral** approach moves from **specific to general** (Mager). [SRC-0109, Ch. 10 "Formulating learning objectives"]
- **Mager's behavioral objective** has three features: an **observable behavior**, the **conditions** of performance, and a **minimum acceptable level** (criterion). Example criterion: "100 per cent accuracy within 15 minutes". [SRC-0109, Ch. 10 "From specific to general: behavioral objectives"]
- Objectives describe what **students** will do, not what the teacher will do; planning needs both long-term goals and short-term objectives. [SRC-0109, Ch. 10 "Formulating learning objectives"]

**Bloom's taxonomy**
- Developed by a committee chaired by **Benjamin Bloom (1956)**; domains: **cognitive, affective, psychomotor**. [SRC-0179, lead]
- Original cognitive levels: Knowledge, Comprehension, Application, Analysis, **Synthesis, Evaluation**. **2001 revision:** **Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create** (renamed, and the top two reordered). [SRC-0179, lead and "Cognitive"]
- The affective handbook appeared in **1964**; **Elizabeth Simpson** (1972) proposed a seven-level psychomotor taxonomy. [SRC-0179, "History", "Psychomotor"]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Tyler starts with objectives; UbD starts with results and evidence.** Both are "ends first", but UbD puts **assessment before activities**.
- **Spiral ≠ repetition.** Topics return at a **higher level** each time.
- **K–12 has 6 years of secondary** (4 JHS + 2 SHS), not 4.
- **MTB-MLE is no longer the K–3 medium of instruction** (RA 12027, 2024), though it may continue in qualifying monolingual classes.
- **"The teacher will explain…" is not an objective** — objectives state learner behavior.
- **Revised Bloom: Create is highest**, Evaluate second; in 1956 Evaluation was highest and Synthesis below it.
- **Hidden curriculum is unintended**, not "secret content".

## 4. Memory aid

**Tyler "POOE"**: Purposes, Opportunities (experiences), Organization, Evaluation.
**UbD "Results → Evidence → Activities"** ("REA" — Really End At the start).
**Mager "ABC-D" shortcut: Behavior, Condition, Degree.**
**Revised Bloom "Remember Understand Apply Analyze Evaluate Create" — "Real Understanding Always Achieves Excellent Creations."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0021 RA 10533 (Secs. 4–6); SRC-0022 RA 12027 (Secs. 1–2)
- SRC-0109 Seifert & Sutton, *Educational Psychology* 2e (CC BY 3.0), Ch. 10
- SRC-0177 Ralph W. Tyler; SRC-0178 Understanding by Design; SRC-0179 Bloom's taxonomy; SRC-0180 Spiral approach; SRC-0181 Hidden curriculum — Wikipedia (tertiary)
- SRC-0001 Res. 11 s. 2025 (ProfEd TOS)

title: Methods and strategies of teaching — teacher-directed and student-centered strategies, new literacies, lesson planning
md:
# PE-B2 — Methods and strategies of teaching

Section B is 45 items; our working split gives this line about **15 items**. Outcomes: **new literacies** (multicultural, social, media, financial, cyber/digital, eco, arts and creativity) and **developmentally sequenced lesson plans** on the K to 12 spiral curriculum. [SRC-0001, Annex A, ProfEd B] With 25 Apply items in Section B, expect "which strategy best fits this class" scenarios.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Two families of strategies.** **Teacher-directed** (lecture with advance organizers, mastery learning, direct instruction, Madeline Hunter's effective teaching model) organize content for the learner. **Student-centered** (independent study, inquiry/discovery, cooperative learning, project-based learning) let learners direct more of the work. Good teachers mix them.

**Choosing.** Choose by the kind of thinking you want, how much the content must be organized for learners, and how much responsibility learners can take.

**New literacies** extend "reading and writing" to media, digital tools, money, the environment, other cultures and social settings. Each is a set of skills: to **access, analyze, evaluate and create**.

**Lesson sequencing** follows K to 12's spiral progression (RA 10533): start from what learners know, move to the unknown, and revisit at greater depth.

## 2. Testable facts

**Teacher-directed strategies (Seifert & Sutton Ch. 9)**
- **Lecture/exposition:** telling or explaining previously organized information. Students may look passive but must make an effort to listen to learn. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 "Lectures and readings"]
- **Advance organizers (Ausubel, 1978):** brief verbal or graphic overviews of material before it is presented, which partially organize the material for students. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 "Advance organizers"]
- **Concept maps:** diagrams of relationships among concepts, usually made by the student. Outlining and note-taking also help learners organize expository material. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 Table 24 and "Concept maps"]
- **Mastery learning:** **all students learn to the same high level**, though some take longer. Typical cycle: brief lesson → **ungraded test** → enrichment for those who mastered it, **tutoring or extra materials** for others → retest. Challenges: fairness of enrichment vs remediation, and the need for a detailed, organized curriculum of small units. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 "Mastery learning"]
- **Direct instruction** (often): a **highly scripted** version of mastery learning (Engelmann) mixing behaviorism (immediate explicit praise) and cognitive theory (stated objectives, frequent review); small logical steps with ample practice. Very effective for **basic skills** such as early reading and arithmetic, especially in **K–3**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 "Direct instruction"]
- **Madeline Hunter's effective teaching model (mastery teaching):** **prepare students to learn** (use the start of the lesson, advance organizers, explicit objectives); **present information clearly** (a set structure, familiar examples, concise); **check for understanding and give guided practice** (questions everyone answers, choral responses, sampling individuals); **provide for independent practice** (do the first few together; keep practice brief with feedback). [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 Table 25]

**Student-centered strategies**
- **Inquiry learning** (also called discovery learning, Bruner; progressive education, Dewey): the teacher poses thoughtful questions and **does not answer them directly**, guiding students to investigate. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 "Inquiry learning"]
- **Cooperative learning:** groups rewarded partly or wholly for **group success**. Students need time and a place to work together. If a group grade goes to the whole group only, **freeloading** is possible; if only to individual contributions, **overspecialization** can occur. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 "Cooperative learning"]
- **Jigsaw (Aronson & Patnoe; Slavin):** each member becomes an **expert** on one part in an expert group, then teaches it back to the home group. **STAD (Student Teams–Achievement Divisions, Slavin):** teams of 4–5 study together; students are tested individually and **scored partly on improvement**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 Table 26; Ch. 6 jigsaw passage]
- **Project-based learning (Katz):** a question or problem of interest is investigated together over **extended periods**, ending in a presentation, report or product. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 Table 26; Ch. 6 jigsaw passage]
- Choosing a strategy depends on the forms of thinking to encourage, how much ideas must be organized by the teacher, and how much **responsibility** students should take for directing their own learning. [SRC-0109, Ch. 9 "Instructional strategies: an abundance of choices"]

**New literacies**
- **Media literacy:** the ability to **access, analyze, evaluate and create** media in various forms, and to reflect critically and **act ethically**. [SRC-0182, lead and goals paragraph]
- **Digital literacy:** the ability to **find, evaluate and communicate** information using digital devices and platforms; first defined by **Paul Gilster (1997)**. **Henry Jenkins** distinguished the **participation gap** from the digital divide. [SRC-0184, lead, "History", "Participation gap"]
- **Financial literacy:** the skills, knowledge, behavior and attitude that let a person make **informed decisions about money**. [SRC-0183, lead]
- **Ecological literacy (ecoliteracy):** understanding the natural systems that make life possible and using ecological principles to build **sustainable communities**; developed by **David Orr and Fritjof Capra** in the 1990s. [SRC-0185, lead]
- **Social literacy** (sociocultural view): literacy learned through **social interaction** with peers and adults, using books, games, conversations, field trips and stories. [SRC-0187, lead]
- **Multicultural education:** strategies that teach the histories, cultures and contributions of diverse groups. **James Banks's** dimensions: **content integration, knowledge construction, prejudice reduction, equity pedagogy, empowering school culture**. [SRC-0186, lead and "Implementation"]

**Sequencing lessons in K to 12**
- The curriculum uses the **spiral progression** approach and pedagogies that are **constructivist, inquiry-based, reflective, collaborative and integrative**; it proceeds **from the known to the unknown**. [SRC-0021, Sec. 5(e)–(g)]
- Objectives should be sequenced through the cognitive levels (revised Bloom: **Remember → Understand → Apply → Analyze → Evaluate → Create**). [SRC-0179, "Cognitive"]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Mastery learning ≠ Hunter's mastery teaching.** Mastery learning = everyone reaches the same high level with variable time; Hunter's model = a lesson-delivery sequence.
- **Direct instruction is not "lecture".** It is scripted, small-step, practice-heavy and praise-rich.
- **Inquiry: the teacher withholds the answer** and asks further questions.
- **Jigsaw = expert groups; STAD = improvement points.**
- **Advance organizer comes before** the new material, not after.
- **Media literacy includes creating** media, not only analyzing it.
- **Prejudice reduction and equity pedagogy are different Banks dimensions**: attitudes vs teaching methods that help diverse groups achieve.

## 4. Memory aid

**Hunter "Prepare, Present, Check, Practice."**
**Banks "CK-PEE"**: Content integration, Knowledge construction, Prejudice reduction, Equity pedagogy, Empowering school culture.
**Media literacy "AAECA"**: Access, Analyze, Evaluate, Create, Act.

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0109 Seifert & Sutton, *Educational Psychology* 2e (CC BY 3.0), Ch. 9
- SRC-0182 Media literacy; SRC-0183 Financial literacy; SRC-0184 Digital literacy; SRC-0185 Ecological literacy; SRC-0187 Social literacy; SRC-0186 Multicultural education; SRC-0179 Bloom's taxonomy — Wikipedia (tertiary)
- SRC-0021 RA 10533 Sec. 5
- SRC-0001 Res. 11 s. 2025

title: Educational technology, learning resources and classroom management — including learners from indigenous groups
md:
# PE-B3 — Educational technology, resources and classroom management

Section B is 45 items; our working split gives this line about **15 items**. Outcomes: strategies, materials, technology and **classroom management**, including for **learners from indigenous groups**; use of **conventional and non-conventional resources including ICT**. [SRC-0001, Annex A, ProfEd B] HE-A7 covers TPACK, CRAAP, gamification and adaptive learning; this lesson adds media selection, management and IP education.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Choosing resources.** Edgar Dale's **Cone of Experience** orders media from **concrete** (direct experience) to **abstract** (verbal symbols). It is a guide to concreteness, not a retention chart. Technology helps most when it fits content and pedagogy (TPACK).

**Managing a class is mostly prevention.** Arrange space for learning, set **procedures** (routines for repeated tasks) and a few **rules** (standards of behavior), plan **transitions**, and stay **"withit"** — aware of everything going on — so you can deal with several things at once (**overlapping**).

**Responding to misbehavior** goes from mild to strong: ignore minor behavior that will not spread; use gestures, eye contact and proximity; use **natural and logical consequences**; for conflicts, use Thomas Gordon's steps: decide **who owns the problem**, **active listening**, **assertive I-messages**, then **negotiation**.

**Indigenous learners.** Under IPRA (RA 8371), the State provides an integrated, culturally relevant education to IP children and respects their right to education in their own language and cultural ways of teaching.

## 2. Testable facts

**Media and technology**
- **Edgar Dale** introduced the **Cone of Experience** in **1946** (revised **1954, 1969**) as an intuitive model of the **concreteness** of audiovisual media. Dale included **no percentages** and warned against taking it too literally; the "remember 10% of what you read" numbers came later (Treichler, 1967). [SRC-0148, "Cone of Experience"]
- TPACK: effective integration needs the overlap of **technological, pedagogical and content knowledge**. [SRC-0144, lead]
- Even a **single classroom computer** can present assignments, enrich students with special interests, and give extra review; more technology helps the teacher move from "full-frontal teaching" to "guide on the side". [SRC-0109, Ch. 1 "New trend #2"]
- Gamification uses game elements (points, badges, leaderboards, feedback, levels); adaptive learning uses algorithms to tailor content to each learner. [SRC-0146, lead; SRC-0147, lead]

**Preventing problems (Seifert & Sutton Ch. 7)**
- **Arranging space:** whatever the layout, it should help students focus and minimize distraction. Displays should reinforce curriculum and recognize student work, but **too many make a room busy**; decorate some space and leave some for later. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Arranging classroom space", "Displays and wall space"]
- **Procedures/routines** are specific ways of doing common, repeated tasks (e.g. handing in homework); they are like **social conventions**. **Rules** express **standards of behavior** for which students take personal responsibility. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Establishing daily procedures and routines", "Establishing classroom rules"]
- Keep rules **few** (the sample lists five) and general. There is a **stronger case for involving students in making rules** than in making procedures, because rules concern personal responsibility. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Establishing classroom rules"]
- **Transitions** are times of lost time and likely misbehavior; plan them. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Managing transitions"]
- **Withitness (Kounin, 1970):** awareness of everything happening in the classroom at once; experienced teachers show it more. It makes **overlapping** possible — responding to several nearly simultaneous events. Merely showing you are "withit" can deter off-task behavior. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "withitness" passage]
- **Ripple effect (Kounin):** misbehavior left alone can be contagious. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Responding to student misbehavior"]

**Responding to misbehavior**
- **Ignoring** may be wise when the behavior is minor and unlikely to disrupt others. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Ignoring misbehaviors"]
- **Gestures, eye contact and body language** can redirect students with little or no talk; young children and students from other cultures may misread nonverbal cues. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Gesturing nonverbally"]
- **Natural consequences** happen without anyone's intention (a late student misses material). **Logical consequences** are imposed by others but clearly related to the act (a student who steals a lunch repays it). Both can be effective. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Natural and logical consequences"]
- **Thomas Gordon, Teacher Effectiveness Training:** first decide **problem ownership** — the owner is the person primarily troubled by the behavior (student, teacher, or another student), who takes primary responsibility for solving it. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Step 1: clarifying and focusing: problem ownership"]
- **Active listening:** attend to all of what a student says and keep checking your understanding with questions. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Step 2: active, empathetic listening"]
- **Assertive discipline and I-messages:** comments should be **assertive** (neither passive nor hostile; Canter) and use **I-messages** (Gordon), which state how the behavior affects the teacher, e.g. "Your talking is making it hard for me to remember what I'm saying." [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Step 3: assertive discipline and I-messages"]
- **Negotiation** for persistent conflicts: define the problem (with active listening), **brainstorm solutions with the student**, choose and try one, and evaluate. [SRC-0109, Ch. 7 "Step 4: negotiation"]

**Indigenous peoples' education (IPRA, RA 8371)**
- The State, through the **NCIP**, provides a complete, adequate and **integrated system of education relevant to the needs** of IP children and youth. [SRC-0036, Sec. 28]
- The State respects IPs' right to **preserve and protect their culture, traditions and institutions**. [SRC-0036, Sec. 29]
- The State provides **equal access** to educational opportunities **without prejudice** to IPs' right to establish and control their own educational systems, providing education **in their own language** and in a manner **appropriate to their cultural methods of teaching and learning**; IP children have the right to all levels and forms of State education. [SRC-0036, Sec. 30]

**Safe classrooms**
- The Anti-Bullying Act requires schools to adopt anti-bullying policies (see PE-A2). [SRC-0025, Sec. 3]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Dale's Cone is not a retention pyramid.** No percentages are Dale's.
- **Procedures ≠ rules.** Lining up for lunch is a procedure; "respect others' property" is a rule.
- **Withitness vs overlapping.** Withitness is awareness; overlapping is handling two things at once.
- **Natural vs logical.** Natural = no one imposes it; logical = someone imposes it, but it fits the act.
- **I-message vs You-message.** "I can't hear the group when there's talking" (I-message) vs "You're so noisy" (You-message).
- **Problem ownership first.** If only the teacher is bothered, the teacher owns the problem.
- **IP education under IPRA** includes the right to the IP's own language and cultural methods, not only "access to regular schools".

## 4. Memory aid

**Gordon's four steps "O-L-I-N"**: Ownership, Listen, I-message, Negotiate.
**Kounin "With-It, Overlap, Ripple."**
**Consequences: "Nature happens; Logic is given."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0109 Seifert & Sutton, *Educational Psychology* 2e (CC BY 3.0), Ch. 1, Ch. 7
- SRC-0148 Edgar Dale; SRC-0144 TPACK; SRC-0146 Gamification; SRC-0147 Adaptive learning — Wikipedia (tertiary)
- SRC-0036 RA 8371 (Secs. 28–30); SRC-0025 RA 10627
- SRC-0001 Res. 11 s. 2025

title: The child and adolescent learner — development and learning principles
md:
# PE-C1 — The child and adolescent learner: development and learning principles

Section C of the Professional Education outline (30 items, 20% of the part) asks you to use **student-centered, metacognitive, inclusive and developmentally appropriate** pedagogy. It also asks you to read the learning environment, differentiate teaching, and "draw implications of research findings related to child development along biological, cognitive, linguistic, socio-cultural dimensions" [SRC-0001, ProfEd Section C]. Most items are at the *Apply* level (15 of 30), so expect classroom scenarios. Know each theory well enough to recognize it in action.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Development theories** describe how people change.
- **Piaget:** thinking develops in four stages, from learning through the senses to abstract reasoning.
- **Vygotsky:** thinking grows through social interaction. A learner can do more with help than alone (the zone of proximal development), and the helper gradually removes the support (scaffolding).
- **Erikson:** personality develops through eight psychosocial "crises" across the whole lifespan, each resolved toward a strength such as trust or identity.
- **Kohlberg:** moral reasoning moves from avoiding punishment, to caring what others think, to principles like justice.
- **Bronfenbrenner:** the child sits inside nested systems, from family and school out to culture, all moving through time.
- **Freud:** an older theory of psychosexual stages, now widely disputed.

**Learning theories** describe how learning happens.
- **Classical conditioning (Pavlov):** a neutral signal becomes linked to something that already triggers a reflex.
- **Operant conditioning (Skinner, building on Thorndike's law of effect):** consequences change how often a behavior happens.
- **Observational learning (Bandura):** we learn by watching others.
- **Memory (information processing):** information passes through sensory, short-term and long-term memory.
- **Motivation:** it can come from inside (intrinsic) or outside (extrinsic). Maslow's hierarchy puts survival needs at the base and self-actualization at the top.
- **Multiple intelligences (Gardner):** at least eight kinds of intelligence. Educators use it widely, but cognitive psychologists criticize its lack of evidence.

**For the classroom:** a secondary teacher's learners are mostly in Piaget's formal-operational stage and Erikson's identity stage. Lessons can use hypotheticals and abstract reasoning, and should give room for identity questions. Lessons should also be scaffolded, socially rich and fair to diverse learners.

## 2. Testable facts

**Piaget (cognitive stages)**
- Piaget's four stages, with typical ages: **sensorimotor 0–2**, **preoperational 2–6**, **concrete operational 7–11**, **formal operational 12+**. [SRC-0087, 1.3 Table 1.2]
- Sensorimotor: the world is experienced through senses and actions. Key issues: **object permanence**, stranger anxiety. [SRC-0087, 1.3 Table 1.2]
- Preoperational: uses words and images to represent things but lacks logical reasoning. Key issues: **pretend play, egocentrism**, language development. [SRC-0087, 1.3 Table 1.2]
- Concrete operational: understands concrete events and analogies logically and performs arithmetic operations. Key issue: **conservation**. [SRC-0087, 1.3 Table 1.2]
- Formal operational: **abstract reasoning**, abstract logic, moral reasoning. [SRC-0087, 1.3 Table 1.2]

**Vygotsky (sociocultural)**
- Vygotsky emphasized the role of **social interaction** in cognitive development. [SRC-0087, 1.3]
- **Zone of proximal development (ZPD):** concepts just beyond a learner's current ability that they are ready to master with a little help, often from others. [SRC-0087, 1.3]
- **Scaffolding:** support that helps a learner achieve beyond their current level and is **gradually withdrawn** as they become more competent (e.g. training wheels on a bicycle). [SRC-0087, 1.3]

**Erikson (psychosocial stages)**
- Erikson built on Freud's psychosexual theory and proposed a **psychosocial** theory. Each stage poses a "psychosocial crisis" between the individual and society's expectations. [SRC-0087, 1.3]
- Erikson's eight stages and ages: **trust vs mistrust (0–1)**; **autonomy vs shame/doubt (1–3)**; **initiative vs guilt (3–6)**; **industry vs inferiority (7–11)**; **identity vs confusion (12–18)**; **intimacy vs isolation (19–29)**; **generativity vs stagnation (30–64)**; **integrity vs despair (65+)**. [SRC-0087, 1.3 Table 1.1]
- Identity vs confusion (adolescence): experimenting with and developing identity and roles. [SRC-0087, 1.3 Table 1.1]
- Industry vs inferiority (school age): self-confidence when competent, or a sense of inferiority when not. [SRC-0087, 1.3 Table 1.1]

**Kohlberg (moral reasoning)**
- Kohlberg extended Piaget's work on moral reasoning and studied responses to dilemmas such as the **Heinz dilemma**. He cared about the **reasoning**, not the yes/no answer. [SRC-0086, 9.2]
- Three levels: **pre-conventional** (decisions based on consequences to oneself: avoid punishment, be obedient, get a reward); **conventional** (judging by what others think, or by law and order); **post-conventional** (internalized principles such as justice and compassion). [SRC-0087, 8.2]
- Typical timing: pre-conventional before about age 9–10; conventional from early adolescence; post-conventional once formal operational thought is reached, and only a few fully achieve it. [SRC-0086, 9.2; SRC-0087, 8.2]

**Bronfenbrenner (ecological systems)**
- **Microsystem:** settings the person directly experiences, such as family, peers, school and teachers. [SRC-0087, 1.4]
- **Mesosystem:** interactions *between* microsystems, e.g. parent–teacher communication. [SRC-0087, 1.4]
- **Exosystem:** settings that affect the person indirectly, e.g. a parent's workplace policy that changes home life. [SRC-0087, 1.4]
- **Macrosystem:** culture, beliefs, ideologies, laws, economic systems and values. [SRC-0087, 1.4]
- **Chronosystem:** all levels change together through historical time. [SRC-0087, 1.4]

**Freud (psychosexual)**
- Five stages: **oral (0–1)**, **anal (1–3; conflict over toilet training)**, **phallic (3–6)**, **latency (6–12)**, **genital (12+)**. Most of Freud's ideas have not found support in modern research. [SRC-0086, 9.2 and 11.2 Table 11.1]

**Behaviorism and social learning**
- Classical conditioning (Pavlov): an **unconditioned stimulus** (meat powder) produces an **unconditioned response** (salivation). A **neutral stimulus** (a tone) presented just before it comes to trigger the response. [SRC-0086, 6.2]
- Skinner's operant conditioning built on **Thorndike's law of effect**: the consequences of an action alter how often it happens. [SRC-0087, 1.3]
- **Reinforcement increases** a behavior; **punishment decreases** it. **Positive** = something is *added*; **negative** = something is *removed*. [SRC-0086, 6.3 Table 6.2]
- A **variable-ratio** schedule (reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses, e.g. gambling) gives a high, steady response rate and the **slowest extinction**. [SRC-0086, 6.3]
- **Bandura:** observational learning, i.e. learning by watching others. [SRC-0087, 1.3]

**Intelligence, memory, motivation**
- **Gardner:** at least eight intelligences: linguistic, logical-mathematical, musical, bodily-kinesthetic, spatial, interpersonal, intrapersonal, naturalistic. The theory is criticized by cognitive psychologists for lacking empirical evidence, though educators still use it. [SRC-0086, 7.4]
- **Atkinson–Shiffrin (1968)** memory model: information passes through **sensory memory → short-term memory → long-term memory**. Long-term capacity is believed to be unlimited. [SRC-0086, 8.1]
- Short-term memory is a temporary store and is a *component* of working memory; the two terms are not exactly the same. [SRC-0086, 8.1]
- **Intrinsic** motivation comes from internal satisfaction; **extrinsic** motivation is about getting something from others. [SRC-0086, 10.1]
- **Maslow (1943):** physiological needs at the base, then safety, love and belonging, and self-worth (esteem), with **self-actualization** at the top. It can be realized only when lower needs are met. [SRC-0086, 10.1]

**Early years**
- The Early Years Act (RA 10410) recognizes ages **0 to 8** as the first crucial stage of educational development. [SRC-0074, title]

**Motivation and learner differences (second pass, Stage 5; Seifert & Sutton Ch. 4–6)**
- **Intrinsic motivation** comes from within the learner; **extrinsic motivation** is a tendency to direct attention and energy that originates **outside** the learner. [SRC-0109, Ch. 6 (Student motivation)]
- **Self-efficacy** is the belief that you can carry out a specific task or reach a specific goal (like confidence, defined more precisely). Very low self-efficacy can lead to **learned helplessness**, a perceived complete lack of control over mastering a task. [SRC-0109, Ch. 6 (Student motivation)]
- Attributions about success and failure vary in **locus** (internal, e.g. ability, vs external, e.g. an easy test), **stability** (ability is stable; effort is unstable), and **controllability** (effort is controllable) (Weiner). [SRC-0109, Ch. 6 (Student motivation)]
- **Mastery goals** sustain interest in a subject better than **performance goals**; competitiveness of performance goals can produce negative byproducts. [SRC-0109, Ch. 6 (Student motivation)]
- **Self-determination theory:** motivation runs on a continuum from highly extrinsic to highly intrinsic, and depends on three basic needs: **autonomy, competence, relatedness**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 6 (Student motivation)]
- Carole **Ames's TARGET** model integrates motivation ideas: **Task, Authority, Recognition, Grouping, Evaluation, Time**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 6 (Student motivation)]
- **Field-dependent** learners perceive globally; **field-independent** learners prefer analytic work and working alone. The term "learning styles" may imply more consistency across situations than really exists. [SRC-0109, Ch. 4 (Student diversity)]
- The most frequent special need is **learning disabilities**, impairments in specific aspects of learning, especially **reading**; **ADHD** is a problem with **sustaining attention and controlling impulses**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 5 (Students with special educational needs)]
- Inclusion expects teachers to provide **alternative assessment**, a **least restrictive environment**, and to help create **individual educational plans (IEPs)**; in the US the trend accelerated with the **IDEA (1975, amended 2004)**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 5 (Students with special educational needs)]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Mixing up Piaget and Erikson.** Piaget = *thinking* (cognitive). Erikson = *personality and social* crises. "Object permanence" and "conservation" are Piaget; "trust" and "identity" are Erikson.
- **Stage-age boundaries vary by book.** One OpenStax table gives preoperational as 2–6 and concrete as 7–11; many reviewers say 2–7. Exam items normally test *order and features*, not exact edge ages. Learn the order and the hallmark of each stage.
- **Negative reinforcement is not punishment.** Negative reinforcement *removes* something unpleasant to *increase* a behavior. Punishment *decreases* a behavior.
- **ZPD vs scaffolding.** The ZPD is the *zone*: what a learner can do with help. Scaffolding is the *support* given inside it, which is then withdrawn.
- **Mesosystem vs exosystem.** Mesosystem = two of the child's own settings interacting (home and school). Exosystem = a setting the child is not in that still affects them (a parent's workplace).
- **Kohlberg's conventional level** is about what others think, or rules and laws. Following a principle *against* the law is post-conventional.
- **Freud is not Erikson.** Freud: psychosexual, five stages, ends at genital. Erikson: psychosocial, eight stages, across the lifespan.

## 4. Memory aid

**Piaget: "Smart Penguins Count Fish"** — Sensorimotor, Preoperational, Concrete, Formal.
**Erikson: "TAI-II-GI"** — Trust, Autonomy, Initiative, Industry, Identity, Intimacy, Generativity, Integrity.
**Bronfenbrenner: "My Mom Expects Many Chores"** — Micro, Meso, Exo, Macro, Chrono, from closest to widest, then time.

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0109 Seifert & Sutton, *Educational Psychology* 2e (CC BY 3.0), Ch. 4–6 (second pass)

- SRC-0087 OpenStax *Lifespan Development* (2024), sections 1.3, 1.4, 8.2 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
- SRC-0086 OpenStax *Psychology 2e* (2020), sections 6.2, 6.3, 6.4, 7.4, 8.1, 9.2, 10.1, 11.2 (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)
- SRC-0074 RA 10410 Early Years Act
- SRC-0001 PRC Res. 11 s. 2025 TOS (ProfEd Section C)

**Not yet covered here (need sources):** Gestalt, the details of Thorndike's laws of readiness and exercise, Bruner's modes, and Bloom's taxonomy (planned for PE-B2).

title: Assessment of learning — validity, reliability, bias, test construction, scoring, basic statistics and interpreting scores, feedback
md:
# PE-D1 — Assessment of learning

ProfEd Section D is **22 items** (15%; Remember 3, Understand 3, Apply 12, Analyze 2, Evaluate 1, Create 1). Outcomes: traditional and authentic assessment; formative and summative tools; **rules of test construction**; product and process assessment; **interpreting results**; **basic statistics**; feedback to learners and parents. [SRC-0001, Annex A, ProfEd D] HE-C1 covers formative/summative, performance assessment, rubrics and portfolios; this lesson covers test quality, item writing, statistics and score interpretation.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Quality of an assessment = validity + reliability + absence of bias.** Validity: are the interpretations of results justified (does it measure what it should)? Reliability: is it consistent? Bias: does it distort scores because of gender, ethnicity or class?

**Item types.** **Selected response** (true-false, matching, multiple choice) is objective and reliable to score but cannot measure every goal. **Constructed response** (completion, short answer, essay) reduces guessing and measures complex outcomes but is harder to score reliably.

**Score interpretation.** **Criterion-referenced**: what the learner can do against a standard. **Norm-referenced**: how the learner compares with others.

**Statistics.** Central tendency: **mean, median, mode**. Spread: **range, standard deviation**. In a **normal curve**, about 68% of scores lie within ±1 SD. Standard scores: **z** (mean 0, SD 1), **T** (mean 50, SD 10), **stanine** (mean 5, SD 2).

**Feedback** should be prompt and specific, telling learners what they did well and what to change.

## 2. Testable facts

**Validity, reliability, bias (Seifert & Sutton Ch. 11)**
- High-quality assessment needs **good validity and reliability and absence of bias**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Selecting appropriate assessment techniques I: high quality assessments"]
- **Validity** concerns the **interpretations and uses** of results (not the test itself) and is a matter of **degree**. Three sources of evidence: **content** (does it cover the intended content and tasks?), **construct** (does it measure the intended construct, e.g. not English proficiency on a math-reasoning test for recent immigrants?), and **criterion-related/predictive** (does it predict later performance, e.g. admission tests and freshman grades?). [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Validity"]
- **Reliability** is the **consistency** of measurement. It increases with **more items/tasks**, **clear directions and tasks**, and **clear scoring criteria**. Example: one confusing item changes a 5-item score by 20% but a 50-item score by only 2%. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Reliability"]
- **Bias:** components that distort performance because of personal characteristics such as gender, ethnicity or social class. Two types: **offensiveness** (negative stereotypes, e.g. all doctors men, all nurses women) and **unfair penalization** (items that depend on background experiences some groups lack). Poor performance alone is not bias. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Absence of bias"]

**Selected response items**
- Selected response items ask learners to **recognize**, not recall; they are **objective** (scoring not influenced by judgment), which raises reliability, but using **only** objective tests can **lower validity** because they do not fit all goals. Assessment must be **aligned to the learning goal** (if the goal is to conduct an experiment, have students conduct one). [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Selected response items"]
- Common item-writing problems: **unclear wording**; **irrelevant cues** (e.g. correct options or true statements are **longer**); **negatives or double negatives**; sentences **copied from the textbook** out of context; **trivial** questions. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Common problems"]
- **True-false:** suits factual knowledge (vocabulary, formulas, dates, names, terms); efficient and easy to write, but **50% chance of guessing**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Strengths and weaknesses"]
- **Matching:** two parallel columns; usually **more options in the second column** so one error does not force another; measures lower-level knowledge (persons–achievements, terms–definitions); hard to make **homogeneous** lists. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Strengths and weaknesses"]
- **Multiple choice** is the most used objective format: it can assess **higher-level thinking** such as application, reduces guessing (four or five options), and does not need homogeneous material. Three steps: a **clearly stated problem in the stem**, **plausible alternatives**, **no irrelevant clues**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Strengths and weaknesses"]
- MCQ errors: the stem does not state the problem (the item becomes a series of true-false statements); options **not grammatically consistent** with the stem; correct answers **clustered in one position** — all positions should be used about equally (but not exactly equally). [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 Table 37]

**Constructed response items**
- Learners **recall and create** answers, so **guessing is reduced**. **Completion** (a statement with a blank) and **short answer** (a question) are answered with a word, phrase, number or symbol. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Constructed response items", "Completion and short answer"]
- **Extended response (essay):** best for **complex outcomes — integration and application** — and assesses writing; easy to write poorly, hard to write well; good prompts make the task clear, sometimes with **planning notes**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Extended response"]
- Scoring essays reliably calls for a **scoring rubric** or point scheme. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Scoring rubrics"]

**Norm- vs criterion-referenced (Ch. 12)**
- **Criterion-referenced** tests measure performance against a **specific standard** (e.g. "mastered 65% of the grade-level problems"); **norm-referenced** tests report performance **relative to others** in a norm group (e.g. percentile). For planning instruction, criterion-referenced information is usually **more useful**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 12 "Basic concepts"]

**Basic statistics (Ch. 12)**
- **Mean** = sum of scores ÷ number of scores; **median** = the middle score (half above, half below); **mode** = the most frequent score (two modes = **bimodal**). [SRC-0109, Ch. 12 "Central tendency and variability"]
- The **mean is strongly affected by extreme scores (outliers)**; the **median is not**, so with extreme scores the median often better shows the typical score. Example: 4, 18, 18, 19, 19, 19, 19, 19, 20, 20 → mean 17.5, median 19. [SRC-0109, Ch. 12 "Central tendency and variability"]
- **Range** = highest − lowest score; it uses only two scores. **Standard deviation** reflects how much, on average, **all** scores deviate from the mean; **variance** is the mean of the squared deviations (SD is its square root). [SRC-0109, Ch. 12 "Central tendency and variability", "Calculating a standard deviation"]
- A **normal distribution** is bell-shaped and **symmetric**; **mean = median = mode**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 12 "The normal distribution"]
- In a normal distribution, **34%** of scores lie between the mean and +1 SD (and 34% between the mean and −1 SD), so **68%** lie within ±1 SD; about **14%** lie between +1 and +2 SD; about **2%** above +2 SD. The mean is the **50th percentile**; **+1 SD is about the 84th percentile**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 12 "The normal distribution"]
- **z-score = (score − mean) ÷ SD**; mean 0, SD 1. Example: IQ 130 with mean 100, SD 15 → z = 2. **T-score:** mean 50, SD 10 (T 70 = z 2). **Stanine:** nine-point scale, mean 5, SD 2, whole numbers only. [SRC-0109, Ch. 12 "Kinds of test scores"]
- **Grade-equivalent** 3.7 = performance expected of a Grade 3 learner in the 7th month; often misunderstood (a 4th grader scoring 6.0 cannot necessarily do 6th-grade work). [SRC-0109, Ch. 12 "Grade equivalent scores"]
- **Qualitative data** are shown with pie charts and bar graphs; **quantitative** data are counts or measurements. [SRC-0091, 1.2]

**Feedback (Ch. 11)**
- Effective feedback is **prompt** (delay lets misconceptions persist), says clearly **what was done well and what needs changing** (not just "good work, A"), and can use **rubrics**; teachers can lessen the focus on grades by putting the grade **after the comments**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Providing feedback"]

**Levels of thinking**
- The LET's own TOS uses the revised Bloom levels **Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create**. [SRC-0179, "Cognitive"; SRC-0001, Annex A]

**Second pass (Stage 5): location, shape and relationship**
- A **quartile** splits data into four parts; the **median is the 50th percentile (2nd quartile)** and the **3rd quartile is the 75th percentile**. [SRC-0090, 8.5]
- When a distribution is **skewed to the left**, the mean is often **less than** the median; **skewed to the right**, the mean is often **greater than** the median; in a **symmetrical** distribution mean, median and mode are close or equal. [SRC-0091, 2.6]
- **Correlation coefficients** range from **−1 to 1** (e.g. −1, −0.97, −0.55, −0.03, 0.61, 0.97, 1); values near ±1 show strong linear relationships, values near 0 almost none. [SRC-0090, 8.8]
- **Correlation does not imply causation** — one of the most common statistical fallacies. [SRC-0090, 8.8]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Validity is about interpretation**, and a test can be reliable but not valid (consistently measuring the wrong thing).
- **Objective ≠ valid.** Objective items are reliable to score but may not fit the goal.
- **Longest option is the answer** is an item-writing flaw (a cue), as are grammatical mismatches and answer-position clustering.
- **Median resists outliers; mean does not.**
- **68% within ±1 SD**, not 50% or 95%. +1 SD ≈ 84th percentile (50 + 34).
- **T = 50 + 10z; stanine mean 5, SD 2.**
- **Criterion-referenced tells what a learner can do**; norm-referenced tells rank.
- *Source caution:* the Seifert & Sutton text contains three slips — Piaget's birth year given as 1880 (it is 1896), z = 2 called the "84th percentile" (z = 1 is), and School A/B SD values that contradict their ranges. Those statements are **not** taught.

## 4. Memory aid

**Quality "VRB": Valid, Reliable, unBiased.**
**Normal curve "34-14-2"** on each side → 68% within ±1 SD.
**Standard scores "z 0/1, T 50/10, Stanine 5/2."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0109 Seifert & Sutton, *Educational Psychology* 2e (CC BY 3.0), Ch. 11–12
- SRC-0091 OpenStax *Introductory Statistics 2e* 1.2, 2.6; SRC-0090 *Contemporary Mathematics* 8.5, 8.8
- SRC-0179 Bloom's taxonomy (Wikipedia)
- SRC-0001 Res. 11 s. 2025

title: Field study and teaching internship — experiential learning, teaching assistantship, portfolio, reflective teaching
md:
# PE-E1 — Field study and teaching internship

ProfEd Section E (Field Study, Teaching Internship and Action Research) is **30 items** (20%); our working split gives this line about **18 items** and PE-E2 about 12. Outcomes: **experiential learning**, **teaching assistantship**, **portfolio**, and **reflective teaching**.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Field study and internship are experiential learning.** You learn by doing, then reflecting, then making sense of it, then trying again — **Kolb's cycle**: concrete experience → reflective observation → abstract conceptualization → active experimentation.

**Reflection is the engine.** Schön distinguishes **reflection-in-action** (while teaching) from **reflection-on-action** (afterwards). Gibbs gives a six-step reflective cycle; Brookfield offers four lenses (your own story, students' eyes, colleagues, theory).

**Student teaching** is the supervised, culminating practice: the intern teaches under a **cooperating teacher** in the school, with a **college supervisor** linking school and college. **Microteaching** scales teaching down (short lesson, small group, recorded) for focused feedback.

**Portfolios** collect evidence of growth and accomplishment; a teaching portfolio usually mixes a working collection with a showcase for an audience.

**Professional growth** continues through colleagues, associations, workshops and reading — and through action research (PE-E2).

## 2. Testable facts

**Experiential learning**
- Kolb's experiential learning model has four stages: **Concrete Experience → Reflective Observation → Abstract Conceptualization → Active Experimentation**. [SRC-0188, "Kolb's experiential learning model" figure]
- Genuine experiential learning requires that the learner be **willing to be actively involved**, able to **reflect**, able to **conceptualize** (analytical skills), and able to **decide and solve problems** using the new ideas. [SRC-0188, "Elements"]
- Experiential learning needs self-initiative, an "**intention to learn**" and an active phase of learning. [SRC-0188, "Implementation"]
- Kolb was influenced by **Dewey, Piaget and Lewin**. [SRC-0189, "Kolb"]

**Reflective practice**
- **Donald Schön**, *The Reflective Practitioner* (**1983**): **reflection-on-action** looks back on an experience and asks what could have been done differently; **reflection-in-action** is reflecting **while** acting. [SRC-0189, lead and "Schön"]
- For Schön, growth begins when practitioners **doubt** their actions and frame situations as problems. [SRC-0189, "Schön"]
- **Gibbs' reflective cycle (1988):** **Description → Feelings → Evaluation → Analysis → Conclusions → Action plan**. [SRC-0189, "Gibbs 1988"]
- **Brookfield (1998)**, four lenses for critical reflection: our **autobiography as learners**, our **learners' eyes**, our **colleagues' experiences**, and **theoretical literature**. [SRC-0189, "Brookfield 1998"]

**Student teaching and microteaching**
- **Student teaching** (teaching practice) is a supervised instructional experience, usually the **culminating course** of a pre-service teacher education program, lasting about a school term. [SRC-0191, lead]
- The student teacher is monitored by the **cooperating teacher** from the host school and by a **college supervisor**, who acts as liaison between the cooperating teacher and the college. [SRC-0191, lead]
- **Microteaching** was invented in **1963** at **Stanford** by **Dwight W. Allen**: a short lesson (originally about **20 minutes**) to a small group is **recorded** and reviewed with peers, a master teacher and students for feedback; class size, time, task and content are **scaled down**. [SRC-0190, lead and "Techniques"]

**Portfolios (Seifert & Sutton Ch. 11)**
- A portfolio is a **purposeful** collection that tells the story of achievement or growth. Dimensions: assessment **for vs of** learning; **progress vs current accomplishments**; **showcase (best work) vs documentation (all work)**; **working vs finished** (a finished portfolio is designed for an audience, such as a job application). [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Portfolios"]

**Professional learning (Seifert & Sutton Appendix C)**
- Resources for reflection fall into four categories: **talking and collaborating with colleagues**, **professional associations**, **professional development workshops and conferences**, and **reading professional literature**. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "Types of resources for professional development"]
- Conversations that stimulate reflection should be about **educational matters**; **group study** among teachers is especially useful for beginning teachers learning from veterans. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "Colleagues as a resource"]

**Licensure context**
- To take the LET an applicant must be a Filipino citizen (or from a country with reciprocity), **at least 18**, in good health and of good moral reputation, not convicted of an offense involving moral turpitude, and a **graduate** of a government-recognized school with the required teacher-education degree. [SRC-0016, Sec. 15]

**Second pass (Stage 5)**
- **Dewey**, on reflection in experiential learning: "successive portions of reflective thought grow out of one another and support one another". Reflection can be **facilitated or independent**. [SRC-0188, "Implementation"]
- **Christopher Johns (1995)** designed structured reflection carried out by **sharing with a colleague or mentor**, "looking in" on one's thoughts and emotions and "looking out" at the situation. [SRC-0189, "Johns 1995"]
- In John **Hattie's** review of evidence (Visible Learning), **microteaching** ranked as the **6th most effective** method for improving student outcomes. [SRC-0190, lead]
- **Student teaching** (for those not yet certified) differs from a **practicum**, taken by already-certified teachers seeking an extension to another specialization; both are college-supervised, field-based experiences. [SRC-0191, lead]
- Professional association meetings and conferences draw on **wider expertise** than one school, but take **effort and money**; balanced professional development also needs frequent, low-cost activities such as **reading professional literature**. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "Professional associations"]
- When reading research, teachers should understand each study's **purpose** and consider **contributing** to professional knowledge themselves through **action research**. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "Reading professional literature"]
- Brookfield's **learners'-eyes** lens often reveals that learners read **diverse meanings** into a teacher's words and actions; **colleagues** act as "critical mirrors". [SRC-0189, "Brookfield 1998"]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Kolb's order**: Experience → Reflect → Conceptualize → Experiment (not Reflect first).
- **In-action vs on-action.** Adjusting mid-lesson when learners look lost = reflection-**in**-action. Writing a journal after class = reflection-**on**-action.
- **Cooperating teacher ≠ college supervisor.** The cooperating teacher is in the host school; the supervisor is from the college.
- **Microteaching is scaled-down and recorded**, not "teaching a micro-topic only".
- **Gibbs starts with Description and ends with Action plan.**

## 4. Memory aid

**Kolb "Every Rider Can Experiment"** = Experience, Reflect, Conceptualize, Experiment.
**Gibbs "Don't Forget Every Amazing Class Activity"** = Description, Feelings, Evaluation, Analysis, Conclusions, Action plan.
**Schön: "in = during, on = after."**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0188 Experiential learning; SRC-0189 Reflective practice; SRC-0190 Microteaching; SRC-0191 Student teaching — Wikipedia (tertiary)
- SRC-0109 Seifert & Sutton, *Educational Psychology* 2e (CC BY 3.0), Ch. 11; Appendix C
- SRC-0016 RA 7836
- SRC-0001 Res. 11 s. 2025

title: Action research — identifying teaching-learning problems, the research cycle, data, ethics, and recommending solutions

# PE-E2 — Action research

Part of ProfEd Section E (30 items); our working split gives this line about **12 items**. Outcome: identify **teaching-learning problems** and **recommend solutions based on research**. [SRC-0001, Annex A, ProfEd E] HE-D1 covers IMRaD, sampling and variables; this lesson goes deeper on what action research is, its cycle, data and ethics.

## 1. Plain explanation

**Action research (teacher research)** is systematic, intentional inquiry by teachers into their **own** practice to improve it. It starts from a real classroom problem, produces knowledge about **this** class, and is shared mainly with **other teachers**.

**The cycle (Mertler):** **plan** (identify the problem, review literature, plan data collection) → **act** (collect and analyze data) → **develop an action plan** (make and document changes) → **communicate and reflect** — then begin again. Lewin, who coined the term in 1944, called it a spiral of planning, action and fact-finding.

**Data** can be simple: student work, observation, video of your own lessons, a teaching journal, interviews. Keep it manageable.

**Ethics.** When results are shared outside the class: protect **privacy** (pseudonyms, change identifying details), get **informed consent**, and respect **freedom to participate**. A teacher's first duty is the students' welfare.

## 2. Testable facts

**Nature of action research (Seifert & Sutton Appendix C; Ch. 1)**
- **Action research** (teacher research) is "systematic, intentional inquiry by teachers for the purpose of **improving their own practice**"; it is **not** the same as research **about** teaching by professional researchers. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "The nature of action research"]
- Defining characteristics: (1) it **originates in problems and dilemmas of classroom practice**; (2) its outcomes are about **particular teachers and classrooms**, not teachers in general; (3) its audience tends to be **other teachers**, giving "insider" perspectives. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "The nature of action research"]
- Supporters argue that focusing on specific contexts makes action research **more credible as practical information**, being attuned to real classrooms. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "The nature of action research"]
- Common assumptions: teaching is itself a **form of research**; action research requires **substantial reflection**; **collaboration** among teachers is crucial; teachers' knowledge should be **shared publicly**. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "Action research in practice"]
- Compared with ordinary good teaching, action research is **planned more thoughtfully, recorded more systematically, and shared more openly**; it reflects and raises teacher professionalism. [SRC-0109, Ch. 1, after Table 1]
- **Kurt Lewin** coined "action research" in **1944**; in 1946 he described "a spiral of steps, each of which is composed of a circle of **planning, action and fact-finding** about the result of the action". [SRC-0169, lead]

**The cycle (Mertler, in Seifert & Sutton Ch. 11)**
- **Planning stage:** (1) **identify and define the problem** — often starting as vague unease and turned into a researchable question; (2) **review related literature**; (3) **develop a research plan** (what data, how and when). [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Cycles of planning, acting and reflecting"]
- **Acting stage:** **collect and analyze data**; data and analyses need not be complex — action research must be **manageable**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Cycles of planning, acting and reflecting"]
- **Developing an action plan:** make and implement changes; **document** actions carefully. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Cycles of planning, acting and reflecting"]
- **Communicating and reflecting:** share results with colleagues, in classes, at conferences or in teachers' journals; reflect ("What did I learn? What should I have done differently? What next?"), which starts a **new cycle**. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Cycles of planning, acting and reflecting"]

**Data sources (Seifert & Sutton Ch. 1, Table 1)**
- Examples of data: **assessing students' assignments**, **observing** students, **interviewing** students, **videotaping one's own teaching**, a **journal diary** by the teacher. Analysis looks for **patterns**, common strengths and problems, then tries changes and observes the result. Results may be reported in a **brief written or oral report to staff**, a journal summary, or shared with students. [SRC-0109, Ch. 1 Table 1]
- Example questions: "How successful are my students at finding high-quality information online?" and "Am I responding to my ESL students as helpfully as to my English-speaking students?" [SRC-0109, Ch. 1 Table 1]
- Report structure for publication commonly follows **IMRaD** (Introduction, Methods, Results, Discussion). [SRC-0168, lead]
- Design vocabulary: explanatory vs response variables, **control group**, **lurking variables**, **convenience vs random samples**. [SRC-0091, 1.2, 1.4]

**Ethics (Seifert & Sutton Appendix C; Ch. 11)**
- Possible **conflict of interest**: a teacher's first priority is **students' welfare**; a researcher's is the field of study. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "Ethical cautions about action research"]
- Ethical issues concern **privacy, informed consent, and freedom to participate**, and arise when results are made **public** or shared outside the classroom. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "Ethical cautions about action research"]
- **Privacy:** use a **pseudonym** and change identifying details in any report or even hallway conversation, without changing essential information. [SRC-0109, Appendix C "Insuring privacy of the student"]
- **Informed consent** form: summarizes the research and data, states participation is **voluntary**, guarantees **confidentiality or anonymity**; students may **decline** research participation even though class work is required. [SRC-0109, Ch. 11 "Ethical issues—privacy, voluntary consent"]
- Learners' education and health data are **sensitive personal information** (RA 10173). [SRC-0045, Sec. 3(l)]

## 3. Common mistakes

- **Action research vs educational research.** Action research is by the teacher, on their own class, to improve their practice; it does not aim to generalize to all schools.
- **Starts with a problem, not a hypothesis from the literature.** The literature review comes after defining the problem.
- **Ends in action and reflection**, not only a report.
- **Ethical rules apply when results go public**; class assessment for teaching does not need consent, research participation does.
- **Pseudonyms are required even in informal talk** about the study.

## 4. Memory aid

**Mertler cycle "Plan → Act → Action plan → Share & Reflect" ("PAAS").**
**Ethics "PIF": Privacy, Informed consent, Freedom to participate.**

## 5. Sources

- SRC-0109 Seifert & Sutton, *Educational Psychology* 2e (CC BY 3.0), Ch. 1, Ch. 11, Appendix C
- SRC-0169 Action research; SRC-0168 IMRAD — Wikipedia (tertiary)
- SRC-0091 OpenStax *Introductory Statistics 2e*
- SRC-0045 RA 10173
- SRC-0001 Res. 11 s. 2025
